event: The fall of the Berlin Wall
note: A garbled announcement that East Germans could travel freely sent crowds to the checkpoints, and by midnight the guards had opened them. The mark is the Brandenburg Gate, where the Wall became the night’s stage.
Parisian crowds stormed the royal fortress-prison to seize its gunpowder, freeing the seven prisoners inside. Its site is now the Place de la Bastille.
The fire began in Thomas Farriner’s bakery on Pudding Lane and burned for four days, destroying some 13,200 houses and old St Paul’s Cathedral.

event: President John F. Kennedy is assassinated
note: Kennedy was shot from the sixth floor of the Texas School Book Depository as his open-top motorcade passed through Dealey Plaza in Dallas.
The uranium bomb ‘Little Boy’ exploded about 600 m above the city centre, near what is now the Atomic Bomb Dome; some 70,000–80,000 people were killed outright.

event: The Titanic sinks on her maiden voyage
note: The liner struck an iceberg about 600 km south-south-east of Newfoundland and sank in under three hours; more than 1,500 people died. The wreck was found in 1985, 3,800 m down.

event: The Declaration of Independence is adopted
note: The Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration in the Pennsylvania State House, now Independence Hall, in Philadelphia.
On the Ides of March, senators stabbed Caesar 23 times in the Curia of Pompey, whose remains lie in the Largo di Torre Argentina in Rome.
About 156,000 Allied troops came ashore on five beaches between the Cotentin peninsula and the mouth of the Orne in Normandy, opening a second front in western Europe.
Japanese carrier aircraft struck the US Pacific Fleet at its base on Oahu, damaging all eight battleships and killing 2,403 Americans; the US declared war the next day.
A botched safety test blew apart Reactor No. 4 and spread radioactive fallout across Europe. The nearby city of Pripyat was evacuated and has stood empty ever since.
Students and workers occupied the vast square in central Beijing for seven weeks; on the night of 3–4 June the army cleared it, killing hundreds or perhaps thousands in the surrounding streets.
Built as the tomb of the pharaoh Khufu on the Giza plateau, it was the tallest structure on Earth for more than 3,800 years.
The emperor Shah Jahan built the white marble mausoleum beside the Yamuna for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth in 1631.
The Inca citadel, probably an estate for the emperor Pachacuti, sits on a ridge high above the Urubamba valley in the Andes of Peru. It was abandoned around the time of the Spanish conquest.
Jørn Utzon’s sail-roofed opera house on Bennelong Point in Sydney Harbour was opened by Elizabeth II after 14 years of building and huge cost overruns.

event: The Statue of Liberty is dedicated
note: France’s gift to the United States, designed by Bartholdi with a frame by Gustave Eiffel, was dedicated on Bedloe’s Island (now Liberty Island) in New York Harbor.

event: The Bolsheviks storm the Winter Palace
note: Red Guards took the Winter Palace in Petrograd, seat of the Provisional Government, with little resistance: the climax of the October Revolution (25 October in the old calendar).
Sultan Mehmed II’s army broke through the land walls after a 53-day siege, ending the Byzantine Empire; the last emperor, Constantine XI, died in the fighting.

event: The first modern Olympic Games open
note: The first Games of the modern era were held in the marble Panathenaic Stadium in Athens, rebuilt on its ancient site. Spyridon Louis, a Greek water-carrier, won the first marathon.
After 27 years in prison, Mandela walked out of Victor Verster Prison near Paarl, then spoke to a huge crowd from the balcony of Cape Town City Hall that evening.
William of Normandy defeated Harold II on a ridge about 10 km inland from Hastings, where the town of Battle and its abbey now stand.
Gandhi was shot by the Hindu nationalist Nathuram Godse on his way to an evening prayer meeting in the garden of Birla House, New Delhi.

event: Hillary and Tenzing reach the summit of Everest
note: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay were the first known climbers to stand on the world’s highest summit, reached by the South Col route from Nepal.
The SS Ancon made the first official transit of the 82 km canal across the Isthmus of Panama, sparing ships the long voyage around South America.
The Red Army encircled and destroyed the German Sixth Army in the ruins of the city on the Volga, a turning point of the war in Europe. The hill of Mamayev Kurgan was fought over for months.

event: The Treaty of Versailles is signed
note: Germany and the Allies signed the peace in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, the room where the German Empire had been proclaimed in 1871.
Colonists protesting the Tea Act boarded three ships at Griffin’s Wharf and dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into Boston Harbor.

event: Britain hands Hong Kong back to China
note: The handover ceremony was held at midnight in the new Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai, ending 156 years of British rule.
The 30 m Art Deco statue was consecrated on the summit of Corcovado, 700 m above Rio de Janeiro.
The emperor Titus opened the Flavian Amphitheatre in Rome with 100 days of games; it could hold perhaps 50,000 spectators.
Napoleon’s Grande Armée marched into an almost deserted Moscow; fires soon destroyed much of the city, and five weeks later he began his disastrous retreat.

event: The first Olympic Games in Asia open
note: The Tokyo Games opened at the National Stadium, showcasing Japan’s recovery from the war; the first bullet train had begun running nine days earlier.
Muhammad’s army entered Mecca almost without bloodshed; he cleared the Kaaba of idols and the city became the holiest site of Islam.
Alexander laid out his new city on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt; under the Ptolemies it became home to the great Library and the Pharos lighthouse.
The 164 km canal joining the Mediterranean and the Red Sea opened with a ceremony at Port Said, attended by the Empress Eugénie of France.

event: Anne Frank’s family goes into hiding
note: The Franks hid in a secret annexe behind Otto Frank’s business on the Prinsengracht for two years, where Anne kept her diary, until they were betrayed in August 1944.

event: Fidel Castro enters Havana in triumph
note: After the dictator Batista fled on New Year’s Day, Castro crossed the island in a week-long victory caravan and entered Havana to cheering crowds.
The temple to Athena on the Acropolis was finished under Pericles as a showpiece of Athenian power, its sculptures overseen by Phidias.

event: Martin Luther King Jr. says “I have a dream”
note: King spoke from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial to some 250,000 people at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.

event: Apollo 11 lifts off for the Moon
note: A Saturn V carried Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins from Launch Complex 39A on Florida’s Space Coast; four days later Armstrong and Aldrin walked on the Moon.
John Wilkes Booth shot Lincoln during a comedy at Ford’s Theatre in Washington, five days after Lee’s surrender; the president died the next morning in a house across the street.
Panic selling on the New York Stock Exchange wiped billions of dollars off share prices within days and helped tip the world into the Great Depression.
On opening day some 200,000 people walked across the bridge over the strait at the mouth of San Francisco Bay, then the longest suspension span in the world.
Built in just over a year on Fifth Avenue in Midtown Manhattan, it stood as the world’s tallest building for nearly forty years.
The first steel-wire suspension bridge joined Manhattan to Brooklyn across the East River after 14 years’ work, during which its designer John Roebling died.

event: The four faces of Mount Rushmore are finished
note: Workers spent 14 years blasting and carving the heads of four presidents, each about 18 m tall, into a granite peak in the Black Hills of South Dakota.
Some 400,000 people came to a dairy farm at Bethel, New York, for three days of music; the town of Woodstock itself is about 70 km away.
Starting in or near the O’Leary family’s barn on the city’s West Side, the fire burned for two days, destroyed some 17,000 buildings and left 100,000 people homeless.
The concrete arch dam across the Black Canyon of the Colorado River, on the Nevada–Arizona border, was finished two years early and created Lake Mead.

event: Russia hands Alaska to the United States
note: The Russian flag came down and the American flag went up at Sitka, the colonial capital, after the United States bought Alaska for $7.2 million, about two cents an acre.
Accusations that began among girls in Salem Village spread across Massachusetts; the colony hanged nineteen people as witches before the trials were halted.

event: The Pyramid of the Sun rises at Teotihuacan
note: The great stepped pyramid dominated the largest city of the ancient Americas, 40 km north-east of modern Mexico City; who built it is still unknown.

event: Rosa Parks refuses to give up her bus seat
note: Her arrest in Montgomery, Alabama, launched a 381-day boycott of the city’s buses led by the young Martin Luther King Jr., which ended in desegregation.

event: Burglars are caught at the Watergate
note: Five men were arrested inside the Democratic National Committee’s offices in the Washington complex; the cover-up that followed forced President Nixon to resign in 1974.
First erected on Mount Lee as an advertisement reading “HOLLYWOODLAND” for a housing estate, it lost its last four letters in 1949.
Walt Disney’s first theme park opened on former orange groves in Anaheim, California; its chaotic first day became known inside the company as “Black Sunday”.

event: Robert E. Lee surrenders at Appomattox
note: Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to Ulysses S. Grant in the parlour of Wilmer McLean’s house in a Virginia village, effectively ending the Civil War.

event: Father Hidalgo’s cry for Mexican independence
note: Miguel Hidalgo rang his church bell in the town of Dolores and called his parishioners to rise against Spanish rule; Mexico celebrates the date as its independence day.
The American battleship blew up in Havana Harbor, killing 260 of her crew; American newspapers blamed Spain, and war followed within weeks.
The Yongle Emperor’s vast walled palace, with some 980 surviving buildings, was home to 24 Ming and Qing emperors until the last abdicated in 1912.
Justinian’s great church, with a dome that seemed to float above it, was finished in under six years and remained the world’s largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years.

event: The Treasury is carved at Petra
note: The Nabataeans cut the façade of Al-Khazneh into a sandstone cliff at the end of the Siq, the narrow gorge leading into their capital in what is now Jordan.
The world’s largest Buddhist monument, nine stacked platforms crowned by 72 stupas, was built under the Sailendra dynasty in central Java and later abandoned to the jungle.

event: Shah Jahan completes the Red Fort
note: The Mughal emperor’s red sandstone palace-fortress in Delhi took nine years to build; India’s prime minister still raises the flag there every Independence Day.
Jawaharlal Nehru spoke to the Constituent Assembly in Delhi’s parliament building on the eve of independence: “at the stroke of the midnight hour … India will awake to life and freedom.”
Christian tradition places Golgotha, the site of the crucifixion and the tomb, within the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem’s Old City.
Tradition holds that the Buddha reached enlightenment under a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya in Bihar; the Mahabodhi Temple now stands beside a descendant of that tree.
The magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck at lunchtime beneath Sagami Bay, and the fires that followed destroyed much of Tokyo and Yokohama; over 100,000 people died.
South Korea’s capital staged the Games at the new Jamsil Olympic Stadium; they were the first in twelve years without a large boycott.
One of the world’s first great cities, with planned streets, drains and a Great Bath, stood by the Indus in what is now Sindh, Pakistan.

event: Darius the Great begins building Persepolis
note: The ceremonial capital of the Persian kings rose on a vast terrace in the Fars region of Iran; Alexander the Great looted it and set its palaces on fire in 330 BC.
Ferdinand Magellan died fighting warriors led by the chieftain Lapulapu on a small island off Cebu; his surviving crew completed the first voyage round the world.

event: The Burma Railway bridge over the Kwai is built
note: Prisoners of war and Asian labourers forced to build the Japanese railway from Thailand to Burma died in their tens of thousands; the bridge at Kanchanaburi still stands.
General Percival surrendered some 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops at the Ford factory in Bukit Timah; Churchill called it the worst disaster in British military history.

event: Ramesses II builds the temples of Abu Simbel
note: Four colossal seated statues of the pharaoh guard the great temple cut into a cliff above the Nile; in the 1960s the temples were cut up and moved 65 m uphill, clear of Lake Nasser.

event: Nelson Mandela becomes South Africa’s president
note: Mandela was sworn in as the country’s first Black president at the Union Buildings in Pretoria, four years after leaving prison, before a crowd of heads of state.

event: Bartolomeu Dias rounds the Cape of Good Hope
note: The Portuguese navigator was blown south past Africa’s tip and saw the cape on his way home, opening the sea route to India that Vasco da Gama followed.
British warships shelled the sultan’s palace in Zanzibar Town until it surrendered after about 40 minutes.

event: The Aswan High Dam is completed
note: The great rock-fill dam across the Nile in southern Egypt tamed the annual flood and created Lake Nasser, one of the largest artificial lakes in the world.

event: The diamond rush at Kimberley begins
note: Diggers found diamonds on Colesberg Kopje in 1871 and dug it away by hand, leaving the Big Hole, one of the largest hand-dug excavations in the world.

event: Gold is found on the Witwatersrand
note: The discovery of the richest goldfield ever found turned a farm on the Highveld into Johannesburg, South Africa’s largest city, within a decade.
In Notre-Dame de Paris, with Pope Pius VII looking on, Napoleon took the crown and placed it on his own head, then crowned Josephine.
Gustave Eiffel’s iron tower on the Champ de Mars was built as the entrance arch to the 1889 World’s Fair and was the tallest structure on Earth until 1930.

event: De Gaulle marches down the Champs-Élysées
note: The day after the German garrison surrendered, Charles de Gaulle led a victory procession from the Arc de Triomphe through cheering crowds.
By legend, Romulus marked out his city on the Palatine Hill after killing his twin, Remus; archaeologists have found huts there from about the same time.

event: The first Olympic Games are recorded at Olympia
note: The Greeks dated their history from the first recorded footrace at the sanctuary of Zeus in the western Peloponnese; the Games were held every four years for over a thousand years.

event: Michelangelo paints the Sistine Chapel ceiling
note: Working on a scaffold beneath the vault of the pope’s chapel in the Vatican, Michelangelo painted more than 300 figures, including the Creation of Adam.
Johannes Gutenberg’s workshop in Mainz printed about 180 copies with movable metal type, beginning the printing revolution in Europe.

event: Work begins on the Leaning Tower of Pisa
note: The cathedral bell tower began to lean on soft ground before its third storey was built; construction took almost two centuries.
Leading Nazis were tried for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Courtroom 600 of the Palace of Justice in Nuremberg; twelve were sentenced to death.
Four weeks after Hitler became chancellor, Germany’s parliament building in Berlin was set ablaze; the Nazis used the fire to suspend civil liberties.
German and Finnish forces cut off the city for 872 days, and perhaps a million civilians died, most of starvation, before the Red Army broke the blockade.
Truman, Stalin and Churchill (later Attlee) met at the Cecilienhof palace outside Berlin to decide how to run defeated Germany.
The coronation in Westminster Abbey was the first to be televised; millions watched on sets bought for the occasion.
England beat West Germany 4–2 after extra time at Wembley Stadium, with Geoff Hurst scoring a hat-trick.

event: The Great Exhibition opens in the Crystal Palace
note: Joseph Paxton’s glass and iron hall in Hyde Park housed some 100,000 exhibits from around the world; six million visitors came in five months.
Ivan the Terrible ordered the church of onion domes on Red Square in Moscow to celebrate his capture of Kazan.

event: Peter the Great founds St Petersburg
note: The tsar laid the first stone of the Peter and Paul Fortress on a Neva island; within a decade the new city replaced Moscow as Russia’s capital.
The Polish Home Army rose against the German occupiers and held out for 63 days; afterwards the Germans systematically razed most of the city.

event: The Second World War begins at Westerplatte
note: The German battleship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on the small Polish garrison guarding the entrance to Gdańsk harbour, which held out for seven days.
When the Soviets blocked the roads to West Berlin, Western aircraft flew in food and coal for eleven months, landing at Tempelhof as often as every 90 seconds.
President Kennedy spoke to some 450,000 people outside Rathaus Schöneberg, West Berlin’s city hall, two years after the Wall went up.

event: The English fleet scatters the Spanish Armada
note: English fireships broke up the Armada’s crescent off Calais, and the battle that followed off Gravelines drove the Spanish fleet north round Scotland.
Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria in a dish he had left out over the summer in his laboratory at St Mary’s Hospital, Paddington, in London.

event: The Beatles play their last concert, on a rooftop
note: The band played for 42 minutes on top of Apple Corps’ offices at 3 Savile Row in London until the police arrived.
After 33½ hours alone over the Atlantic from New York, Lindbergh landed the Spirit of St. Louis at Le Bourget airfield before a crowd of 150,000.

event: The Armistice is signed in a railway carriage
note: Allied and German delegates signed it in Marshal Foch’s carriage in the Forest of Compiègne; Hitler made France sign its 1940 surrender in the same carriage.
The deposed king was beheaded before a crowd in Paris on the square now called the Place de la Concorde.
Britain, France and Italy agreed to let Hitler annex the Sudetenland; Chamberlain flew home promising “peace for our time”.
The first Games in Latin America were opened at the university stadium in the south of the capital; on the podium there, Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised black-gloved fists.
The concrete communications tower on Toronto’s waterfront was the world’s tallest free-standing structure for over thirty years.

event: Blondin crosses Niagara on a tightrope
note: The French acrobat walked a rope strung across the Niagara Gorge below the falls, and came back across it carrying a camera, a chair and later his manager.

event: Roald Amundsen reaches the South Pole
note: Amundsen’s Norwegian party reached the pole with dog sledges 34 days before Robert Falcon Scott’s British team, who all died on the way back.
Filippo Brunelleschi built the double-shelled brick dome without wooden centring; it is still the largest masonry dome in the world.
Leonardo painted the mural in the refectory of the convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, on dry plaster that began to flake within his lifetime.

event: The Louvre opens as a public museum
note: The revolutionary government opened the former royal palace in Paris to the public, with paintings taken from the crown and the Church.
The bascule bridge beside the Tower of London lifts its roadway so that ships can pass upriver to the Pool of London.

event: Work begins on the Sagrada Família
note: Antoni Gaudí took over the Barcelona basilica a year after its foundation stone was laid and worked on it until his death in 1926; it is still being finished.
The Games were held around the stadium on Montjuïc hill, and an archer lit the cauldron with a flaming arrow.
Surrounded American paratroopers held the Belgian road junction during the Battle of the Bulge; asked to surrender, General McAuliffe replied “Nuts!”
Munich celebrated the wedding of Crown Prince Ludwig and Princess Therese with a horse race on a meadow outside the city, named the Theresienwiese after the bride.
The Bavarian king’s fairy-tale castle on a crag above the Pöllat gorge was unfinished when he died in 1886; it opened to paying visitors weeks later.
Begun in 1248 and left unfinished for centuries with a crane on its stump of a tower, the Gothic cathedral was completed to the medieval plans in the 19th century.

event: The first ascent of the Matterhorn
note: Edward Whymper’s party of seven reached the summit above Zermatt, but on the way down a rope broke and four of them fell to their deaths.

event: The Ottoman siege of Vienna is broken
note: King John III Sobieski of Poland led a relief army down the Kahlenberg and routed the Ottoman besiegers, with the largest cavalry charge in history.
Robert the Bruce’s Scots defeated the much larger army of Edward II of England near Stirling Castle, securing Scotland’s independence for a generation.

event: The warship Vasa sinks on her maiden voyage
note: The Swedish king’s top-heavy new warship heeled over and sank in Stockholm harbour less than a mile out; she was raised almost intact in 1961.
The fifth Dalai Lama began the vast white and red palace on the Red Hill in Lhasa, which was the seat of the Dalai Lamas until 1959.

event: The Gateway of India is completed
note: The basalt arch on the Mumbai waterfront commemorated the landing of King George V in 1911; the last British troops to leave India marched through it in 1948.

event: The Buddhas of Bamiyan are carved
note: Two colossal Buddhas, 55 m and 38 m tall, were cut into a sandstone cliff in an Afghan valley on the Silk Road; the Taliban dynamited them in 2001.
Millions of Filipinos filled Epifanio de los Santos Avenue in Manila to protect rebel soldiers, and after four days President Marcos fled to Hawaii.

event: Mandela hands over the Rugby World Cup
note: South Africa beat New Zealand in extra time at Ellis Park, Johannesburg, and Nelson Mandela, wearing the Springbok shirt, presented the trophy to François Pienaar.

event: The Lighthouse of Alexandria is built
note: One of the Seven Wonders, the lighthouse on the island of Pharos guided ships into Alexandria for centuries; the Citadel of Qaitbay stands on its ruins.

event: The Colossus of Rhodes is raised
note: The bronze statue of the sun god Helios, about 33 m tall, stood near the harbour of Rhodes for only 54 years before an earthquake brought it down.
Ice Age artists painted some 600 animals on the walls of a cave in the Dordogne; four teenagers found it in 1940, after their dog fell down a hole.

event: The United Nations moves into its New York headquarters
note: The UN’s glass Secretariat tower rose beside the East River on land bought by John D. Rockefeller Jr. and given to the organisation.
The marble obelisk on the National Mall was begun in 1848, stood unfinished for over twenty years, and on completion was the tallest structure in the world.
Two lanterns hung in the steeple of the Old North Church in Boston warned that British troops were crossing by water, and Revere rode out to raise the alarm.
Hosts Uruguay beat Argentina 4–2 in the Estadio Centenario in Montevideo, built for the tournament and the centenary of the country’s constitution.
The magnitude 9.5 earthquake ruptured nearly 1,000 km of the fault off southern Chile; Valdivia was devastated and its tsunami crossed the Pacific to Hawaii and Japan.
The largest amphibious assault of the Pacific war cost the lives of over 100,000 Japanese soldiers, 12,000 Americans and perhaps a quarter of the island’s civilians.

event: The Ziggurat of Ur is built
note: King Ur-Nammu raised the great stepped temple to the moon god Nanna in the Sumerian city of Ur, in southern Iraq.

event: The palace of Knossos is built
note: The largest Bronze Age palace of the Minoans stood just south of modern Heraklion on Crete; Arthur Evans excavated and partly rebuilt it after 1900.
Built for the Brussels World’s Fair, the steel model of an iron crystal, magnified 165 billion times, was meant to last only six months.

event: Monks found the abbey on Mont-Saint-Michel
note: Benedictine monks settled on the tidal island off the Normandy coast, and over five centuries the abbey rose to crown the rock.

event: Bernadette Soubirous sees the Virgin at Lourdes
note: A 14-year-old miller’s daughter said a lady appeared to her in the grotto of Massabielle; the town in the Pyrenees became one of the great pilgrim sites.

event: The great Temple of Artemis rises at Ephesus
note: Paid for by King Croesus of Lydia, the marble temple was one of the Seven Wonders; a man named Herostratus burned it down in 356 BC to make himself famous.
Some 200,000 people in Rio de Janeiro’s new stadium watched Brazil, needing only a draw, lose the deciding match of the World Cup 2–1 to Uruguay.
A French munitions ship collided with a Norwegian vessel in the Narrows of Halifax harbour, caught fire and blew up, killing nearly 2,000 people.
Gold found on Bonanza Creek in the Yukon drew some 100,000 prospectors north; Dawson City, at the mouth of the Klondike River, grew from nothing into a town of 30,000.

event: The Hindenburg airship bursts into flames
note: The German airship caught fire while mooring at Naval Air Station Lakehurst, New Jersey; 36 people died, and newsreels of the blaze ended the age of passenger airships.
A reactor at the nuclear plant on an island in the Susquehanna River in Pennsylvania partly melted down, the worst accident in American commercial nuclear power.

event: The first shots of the American Civil War
note: Confederate batteries bombarded the federal fort on an island in Charleston Harbor for 34 hours until its garrison surrendered.
Colonial militia met British redcoats on Lexington Green, outside Boston, and the fighting that followed began the American War of Independence.

event: Wolfe defeats Montcalm on the Plains of Abraham
note: British troops climbed the cliffs above the St Lawrence by night and won a short battle outside Quebec City in which both commanders were mortally wounded.
The first Games in the southern hemisphere were centred on the Melbourne Cricket Ground; quarantine rules sent the horse-riding events to Stockholm.

event: Shakespeare’s company builds the Globe Theatre
note: The Lord Chamberlain’s Men built the open-air playhouse on Bankside in Southwark from the timbers of an older theatre; it burned down during a performance of Henry VIII in 1613.
The Roman emperor’s wall ran 117 km across northern Britain from the Solway Firth to the Tyne, with forts and milecastles along its length.

event: The Titanic is launched in Belfast
note: Harland and Wolff’s shipyard launched the liner down its slipway on Queen’s Island before a crowd of 100,000; she was fitted out for another ten months.

event: The Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji is consecrated
note: Emperor Shōmu’s giant bronze Buddha, about 15 m tall, was dedicated in the temple at Nara, Japan’s capital at the time.

event: Jan van Riebeeck founds Cape Town
note: The Dutch East India Company set up a supply station below Table Mountain to grow fresh food for ships sailing to the East Indies.
The US War Department’s five-sided headquarters across the Potomac from Washington was built in only 16 months and is still one of the world’s largest office buildings.
The Massachusetts colony voted to found a college at Newtowne, soon renamed Cambridge; it took its name from John Harvard, who left it his library.
Seattle built the tower with its flying-saucer top for the 1962 World’s Fair; it was finished in less than a year.
Milan’s opera house was built on the site of the church of Santa Maria alla Scala, after the old court theatre burned down.

event: The Great Hypostyle Hall is raised at Karnak
note: Seti I and his son Ramesses II filled the hall in the temple of Amun at Thebes with 134 giant columns; it is now part of Luxor.

event: Temple I is built at Tikal
note: The Maya king Jasaw Chan K’awiil was buried in the steep stone pyramid raised over his tomb in the rainforest of northern Guatemala.
Cortés landed with about 500 men on the Gulf coast, founded the town of Veracruz and scuttled his ships so that none could turn back.
A police raid on the Stonewall Inn in Greenwich Village, New York, sparked days of protest that became a turning point for the gay rights movement.

event: Atomic bombs are tested at Bikini Atoll
note: The United States detonated two atomic bombs among a fleet of target ships in the lagoon of Bikini Atoll in the Marshall Islands, after moving its people away.

event: French agents sink the Rainbow Warrior
note: Two bombs sank Greenpeace’s flagship at her berth in Auckland harbour, killing a photographer; the ship had been about to protest French nuclear tests.

event: A submarine passes under the North Pole
note: The world’s first nuclear-powered submarine crossed the Arctic Ocean beneath the ice from Alaska to Greenland, passing under the pole on the way.

event: The rock churches of Lalibela are carved
note: King Lalibela had eleven churches cut down into the rock of the Ethiopian highlands; the cross-shaped Church of St George is the most famous.

event: Che Guevara is captured in Bolivia
note: Bolivian troops, advised by the CIA, caught the Argentine revolutionary in a ravine and shot him the next day in the schoolhouse of the hamlet of La Higuera.

event: The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus is built
note: The tomb of Mausolus, ruler of Caria, was so magnificent that it gave us the word mausoleum; its stones were later reused in the crusader castle of Bodrum.

event: The Great Mosque of Djenné is rebuilt
note: The largest mud-brick building in the world stands in the Niger floodplain of Mali; townspeople replaster it every year in a festival.

event: King Kashyapa builds his fortress on Sigiriya
note: The king built a palace on top of a 180 m rock in central Sri Lanka, reached through the paws of a giant stone lion.

event: The Qutb Minar rises over Delhi
note: The first sultans of Delhi built the fluted red sandstone tower, 73 m tall, to celebrate the arrival of Muslim rule in northern India.
After a siege of over a year, a Burmese army sacked and burned the island capital of the kingdom of Siam, ending 400 years of its rule.

event: Ulugh Beg builds his madrasa on the Registan
note: Timur’s astronomer grandson built the first of three great tiled madrasas around Samarkand’s central square.

event: Shah Abbas lays out his great square in Isfahan
note: The Safavid shah moved his capital to Isfahan and built one of the largest city squares in the world, framed by mosques, a palace and a bazaar.

event: The Temple of Bel is dedicated at Palmyra
note: The great temple of the Syrian desert city stood for almost 2,000 years before Islamic State blew it up in 2015.
Ash and pumice entombed Pompeii and Herculaneum on the Bay of Naples. Pliny the Younger watched from Misenum across the bay and wrote the only eyewitness account.
Gavrilo Princip shot the heir to Austria-Hungary and his wife Sophie by the Latin Bridge in Sarajevo; within weeks Europe was at war.
The second atomic bomb, aimed at the city centre, exploded over the Urakami valley; about 40,000 people died instantly, and Japan announced its surrender six days later.

event: The Wright brothers make the first powered flight
note: Orville Wright flew 37 m in 12 seconds from the sand dunes at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina: the first controlled, sustained powered flight.

Lee’s invasion of the North was turned back over three days in southern Pennsylvania, ending with the failed Pickett’s Charge. Lincoln gave his Gettysburg Address at the battlefield cemetery that November.

event: Martin Luther publishes his Ninety-five Theses
note: Luther’s attack on the sale of indulgences, traditionally nailed to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg, sparked the Protestant Reformation.
Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Emperor of the Romans at Christmas Mass in Old St Peter’s Basilica, reviving the imperial title in the West.
The crusaders stormed Jerusalem after a five-week siege and massacred much of its population, founding a kingdom that held the city for 88 years.
Hernán Cortés and his Tlaxcalan allies took the island city in Lake Texcoco after a siege of almost three months; Mexico City was built on its ruins.

event: The Mayflower Pilgrims found Plymouth Colony
note: After first anchoring off Cape Cod, the Pilgrims settled at Plymouth in Massachusetts, where about half of them died in the first winter.

event: The great sarsen stones of Stonehenge are raised
note: The sarsen circle and trilithons were raised on Salisbury Plain around 2500 BC, aligned on the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset.
Carter uncovered the steps to the boy king’s almost intact tomb in the Valley of the Kings, on the west bank of the Nile opposite Luxor.

event: Japan signs its surrender aboard USS Missouri
note: Japan’s foreign minister and army chief signed the Instrument of Surrender on the deck of the US battleship anchored in Tokyo Bay, formally ending the Second World War.

event: The Battle of the Somme begins
note: On the first day of the Anglo-French offensive in Picardy the British Army suffered 57,000 casualties, its worst single day; the battle dragged on until November.

Irish republicans seized the General Post Office in Dublin and proclaimed an Irish Republic; the rising was crushed within a week, but the executions of its leaders swung opinion towards independence.

event: The Congress of Vienna redraws Europe
note: Europe’s statesmen remade the continent after Napoleon’s defeat, meeting at the Austrian chancellery on the Ballhausplatz under Metternich amid a famous round of balls.

Guided by Makololo boatmen, the Scottish missionary viewed the great falls of the Zambezi, known locally as Mosi-oa-Tunya, ‘the smoke that thunders’, from an island on their lip and named them after his queen.
An earthquake centred in the Atlantic off south-west Portugal, followed by a tsunami and fires, flattened much of Lisbon on All Saints’ Day and killed tens of thousands.

event: Martin Luther King Jr. is assassinated
note: King was shot on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, where he had come to support striking sanitation workers; the motel is now the National Civil Rights Museum.
Hours after the last US helicopters left, a North Vietnamese tank crashed through the gates of the Independence Palace, ending the Vietnam War.
The earthquake, centred just offshore, and the fires that followed destroyed about 80% of San Francisco; around 3,000 people died.
Khomeini flew home from Paris to a welcome from millions in Tehran; within ten days the Shah’s last government had collapsed.
The volcano in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra blew itself apart; the explosion was heard 4,800 km away, and its tsunamis killed some 36,000 people.
Santa Anna’s Mexican army stormed the old mission held by Texian rebels in San Antonio, killing nearly all its defenders, among them Davy Crockett and Jim Bowie.
Soviet soldiers reached the largest Nazi death camp, beside the Polish town of Oświęcim, and found about 7,000 prisoners still alive; some 1.1 million people had been murdered there.
Leonidas of Sparta and a small Greek force held the narrow coastal pass against Xerxes’ Persian army for three days before being outflanked. Silt has since pushed the coastline kilometres away.
Built for the Khmer king Suryavarman II as a temple to Vishnu, near modern Siem Reap in Cambodia, it is the largest religious monument in the world.

event: China’s first emperor is buried with the Terracotta Army
note: Some 8,000 life-size clay soldiers were buried in pits beside the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, east of modern Xi’an; farmers digging a well found them in 1974.

event: The Hijra: Muhammad leaves Mecca for a new home
note: Muhammad and his followers moved from Mecca to the oasis city of Yathrib, renamed Medina; the year of the Hijra became year one of the Islamic calendar.
Australian and New Zealand soldiers came ashore at a narrow cove on the Gallipoli peninsula, beginning an eight-month campaign that failed to force open the Dardanelles.
More than 338,000 British and French troops were taken off the harbour mole and beaches of Dunkirk, many by a flotilla of small civilian boats.
Kwame Nkrumah declared the Gold Coast independent as Ghana at midnight on the Old Polo Ground in Accra, where his memorial park now stands.

event: Charles Darwin explores the Galápagos Islands
note: HMS Beagle spent five weeks among the volcanic islands, about 900 km off Ecuador; their finches and giant tortoises later helped Darwin towards his theory of natural selection.

event: The moai of Easter Island are carved
note: Nearly all of Rapa Nui’s almost 1,000 moai were carved from the soft volcanic tuff of the Rano Raraku crater, then moved across the island, perhaps ‘walked’ upright with ropes.

event: Brasília becomes the capital of Brazil
note: Brazil moved its capital from Rio de Janeiro to a new city on the central plateau, laid out by Lúcio Costa with buildings by Oscar Niemeyer, built in under four years.

event: Muhammad Ali wins the “Rumble in the Jungle”
note: Ali regained the world heavyweight title by knocking out George Foreman in the eighth round at the 20th of May Stadium in Kinshasa, in what was then Zaire.

event: Soviet tanks crush the Prague Spring
note: Warsaw Pact armies invaded Czechoslovakia to halt the reforms of the Prague Spring; crowds confronted the tanks in Wenceslas Square.
Methyl isocyanate gas leaked from the Union Carbide pesticide plant over the sleeping city of Bhopal; thousands died within days in the world’s worst industrial disaster.

event: Stamford Raffles founds a British trading post
note: Raffles signed a treaty with the Sultan of Johor allowing the East India Company to set up a post at the mouth of the Singapore River, the start of modern Singapore.

event: The State of Israel is proclaimed
note: David Ben-Gurion read the declaration of independence in the Tel Aviv Museum, hours before the British Mandate expired; neighbouring Arab states invaded the next day.

event: Guy Fawkes is caught beneath Parliament
note: Fawkes was arrested guarding 36 barrels of gunpowder in a cellar under the House of Lords, placed to kill James I at the State Opening of Parliament.
A jury of 500 Athenians found the philosopher guilty of impiety and corrupting the young; he drank hemlock in the state prison near the Agora.
By leading a legion across the small river that marked the edge of his province in northern Italy, Caesar started a civil war; the Rubicon is usually identified with the Fiumicino near Savignano.
Alaric’s Visigoths entered through the Salarian Gate and plundered the city for three days, the first time in 800 years that Rome had fallen to a foreign enemy.
Bolsheviks shot the deposed Tsar Nicholas II, his wife, their five children and four servants in the cellar of the Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, in the Urals.
All four Canadian divisions attacked together for the first time and took the ridge north of Arras; a great white memorial now crowns it.
British and American raids started a firestorm that gutted the baroque centre of the Saxon capital and killed about 25,000 people.
Army officers overthrew the Estado Novo dictatorship almost without bloodshed, and the people of Lisbon put carnations in the soldiers’ rifles.
Protestant nobles threw two imperial governors and their secretary out of a window of Prague Castle; all three survived, but the Thirty Years’ War began.
Students marching to the parliament in Budapest began a nationwide revolt against Soviet rule; Soviet tanks crushed it within three weeks.

event: Ceaușescu is booed off his balcony
note: A crowd turned on the dictator during his speech on Bucharest’s Palace Square; four days later he and his wife were tried and shot.
The 17-year-old peasant girl rallied the French to break the English siege of the Loire city, the turning point of the Hundred Years’ War.
Sailors angry at rotten meat seized the ship and sailed into Odessa, where troops fired on the crowds; Eisenstein’s film set the massacre on the city’s great steps.
Giuseppe Garibaldi landed about a thousand red-shirted volunteers at Marsala and within months had conquered the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.
The king stepped out onto a scaffold built against the Banqueting House in Whitehall; England had no monarch for eleven years.

event: Roger Bannister runs the first four-minute mile
note: The 25-year-old medical student ran 3 minutes 59.4 seconds on the Iffley Road track in Oxford.
Cavalry charged a peaceful crowd of some 60,000 gathered on St Peter’s Field in Manchester to demand parliamentary reform, killing at least 15.

event: The Lumière brothers show films to a paying audience
note: The first public screening of their Cinématographe took place in the basement Salon Indien of the Grand Café on the Boulevard des Capucines in Paris.
Along parts of the Western Front around Ypres, British and German soldiers stopped fighting, sang carols and met in no man’s land.

event: Jesse Owens wins four Olympic golds
note: The African-American athlete won the 100 m, 200 m, long jump and relay in Berlin’s Olympic Stadium, at the Games Hitler meant to show off Nazi Germany.
Jewish fighters with a handful of guns held off German troops for almost a month when the SS came to deport the ghetto’s last inhabitants to the death camps.
Prince Felix Yusupov and fellow conspirators killed the tsarina’s mystic adviser at the Moika Palace in Petrograd and dumped his body in the river.
Government soldiers who had been billeted on the MacDonalds of Glencoe for twelve days rose before dawn and killed about 30 of their hosts.
American B-29s dropped incendiaries on the wooden districts east of the Sumida River, killing around 100,000 people in the deadliest air raid in history.
After capturing China’s capital, Japanese troops killed prisoners and civilians for six weeks; estimates of the dead run to 200,000 or more.
In the Tet Offensive, North Vietnamese troops seized the old imperial citadel, and a month of street fighting left much of the city in ruins.

event: Ho Chi Minh declares Vietnam independent
note: Ho Chi Minh read the declaration to a crowd in Ba Đình Square in Hanoi, opening with lines from the American Declaration of Independence.

event: The Khmer Rouge take Phnom Penh
note: Pol Pot’s guerrillas entered the Cambodian capital and within days drove its two million people into the countryside, beginning four years of terror.
Tunku Abdul Rahman read the proclamation in the new Merdeka Stadium in Kuala Lumpur and led the crowd in seven cries of “Merdeka!”
Two days after Japan’s surrender, Sukarno read a short declaration on the porch of his house in Jakarta; four years of war with the Dutch followed.
After the surrender on the Bataan peninsula, Japanese troops forced some 70,000 American and Filipino prisoners to march north from Mariveles; thousands died on the way.
After the Nawab of Bengal took Fort William, British prisoners were locked overnight in its small guardroom and many suffocated; how many is still disputed.
Ten months after leaving Lisbon, the Portuguese fleet anchored off Kappad, near Calicut, opening the sea route from Europe to India round Africa.
The Persian king’s army entered the greatest city of the age, apparently without a fight, and ended the Neo-Babylonian Empire.
Hülegü Khan’s army stormed the capital of the Abbasid caliphate, killed the last caliph and destroyed its libraries, ending Baghdad’s golden age.

event: The Romans destroy the Temple in Jerusalem
note: Titus’s legions ended the Jewish revolt by storming the city and burning the Second Temple; the Western Wall is a surviving part of its platform.
The Prophet Muhammad’s outnumbered followers from Medina defeated a Meccan army at the wells of Badr, the first great victory of Islam.
Saddam Hussein’s tanks overran the small oil-rich emirate in two days; a US-led coalition drove them out in February 1991.

event: Portugal hands Macau back to China
note: The handover ended more than 440 years of Portuguese presence on the small peninsula west of Hong Kong, Europe’s last colony in Asia.
French squares routed the Mamluk cavalry near Embabeh, across the Nile from Cairo, with the Pyramids on the horizon some 15 km away.
Australian and British troops held the Libyan port for 241 days against Rommel’s Afrika Korps; German propaganda called them the Rats of Tobruk, and they adopted the name.
Roosevelt and Churchill met at the Anfa Hotel in Morocco and announced that the Allies would accept nothing less than Germany’s unconditional surrender.
Israeli commandos flew 4,000 km to Uganda’s main airport, on the shore of Lake Victoria, and freed 102 hostages from a hijacked airliner in 90 minutes.

event: Nelson Mandela is sentenced to life
note: At the end of the Rivonia Trial in Pretoria’s Palace of Justice, Mandela and seven others were jailed for life; Mandela spent 18 of his 27 years in prison on Robben Island.
A punitive expedition burned the royal palace of the Kingdom of Benin in southern Nigeria and carried off thousands of bronzes, many still in Western museums.
The first European fort in sub-Saharan Africa traded first in gold and later in enslaved people; it stands on the coast of Ghana.
The Mahdi’s army stormed the Sudanese city after a ten-month siege and killed Gordon two days before a British relief force arrived.
The first great stone building in history, six stacked platforms over the tomb of King Djoser, stands at Saqqara, south of Cairo.
The mosque and school she endowed in the old city of Fez, Morocco, is often called the oldest university still operating in the world.
Moments after winning the California primary, Kennedy was shot in the kitchen pantry of the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles; he died the next day.
He was shot as he began to speak at the Audubon Ballroom in Washington Heights, Manhattan.
Ohio National Guardsmen fired on students protesting the Vietnam War at Kent State University, killing four.
Fire swept the top floors of a garment factory near Washington Square in New York; with doors locked, 146 workers died, most of them young immigrant women.
The shuttle broke apart 73 seconds after launch from Cape Canaveral, killing all seven crew, among them the teacher Christa McAuliffe; the wreckage fell into the Atlantic.

event: Bell makes the first telephone call
note: “Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you,” Alexander Graham Bell said into his new instrument in his Boston workshop.
Canada’s centennial world’s fair, on islands built up in the St Lawrence River, drew 50 million visits in six months.
The magnitude 9.2 earthquake, the strongest in North American history, struck beneath Prince William Sound and shook Anchorage for nearly five minutes.
A storm surge swept over the low island city on the Texas coast and killed between 6,000 and 12,000 people, the deadliest natural disaster in US history.

event: King Pakal is buried at Palenque
note: The Maya king’s jade-masked body lay under a carved stone lid deep inside his pyramid until an archaeologist found the hidden stairway in 1952.
The king of northern Haiti built the largest fortress in the Americas on a mountaintop to guard against a French return.
Much of the pirates’ harbour town at the tip of the Palisadoes spit in Jamaica slid into the sea, and about 2,000 people died.
Francisco Pizarro laid out his “City of Kings” beside the Rímac River near the coast as the capital of Spanish Peru.
A week of meetings at the town hall on the Plaza de Mayo ended Spanish viceregal rule and began Argentina’s road to independence.
Gold miners at Ballarat, Victoria, built a stockade under their Southern Cross flag; troops overran it in a quarter of an hour, but the miners won their demands.
The bushranger, in home-made armour, was captured after a siege at the Glenrowan Inn in Victoria; he was hanged in Melbourne that November.
Thor Heyerdahl’s balsa raft drifted 101 days from Peru before wrecking on the reef of Raroia in the Tuamotus.
US Marines took the tiny island of Betio in three days of some of the bloodiest fighting of the Pacific war.
Over half a million soldiers fought outside Leipzig, the largest battle in Europe before the First World War; defeat drove Napoleon back across the Rhine.
British and Commonwealth troops fought for three months through deep mud to take a ridge a few kilometres east of Ypres, at the cost of some 250,000 casualties.

event: The German fleet scuttles itself at Scapa Flow
note: Interned in the Orkney anchorage after the war, the German crews opened their ships’ seacocks and sank 52 of them in one afternoon.
The only full clash of the British and German battle fleets, in the North Sea off Denmark, cost Britain more ships but kept Germany’s fleet in port for the rest of the war.

event: The Royal Navy sinks the Bismarck
note: Crippled by a torpedo in her steering gear, the German battleship was pounded by British battleships 600 km west of Brest and sank with over 2,000 men.
Allied troops needed four assaults over five months to break the German line below the hilltop monastery, which Allied bombers had reduced to rubble.
For almost seventy years seven popes lived in the walled city on the Rhône, where they built the huge Palais des Papes.
General Jodl signed the unconditional surrender at Eisenhower’s headquarters, a red-brick school in Reims; it took effect at midnight on 8 May.
The French and Sardinians beat the Austrians south of Lake Garda; the suffering of the wounded moved Henry Dunant to found the Red Cross.
A night-long Luftwaffe raid destroyed the centre of the Midlands city, including its medieval cathedral, whose ruined shell still stands beside the new one.
British paratroopers shot 26 unarmed civil rights marchers in the Bogside area of Derry, Northern Ireland; fourteen died.
The Danish king Christian II had some 80 Swedish nobles and churchmen beheaded in Stockholm’s main square, which soon sparked the revolt that made Sweden independent.
The earthquake struck before dawn beneath the strait by Awaji Island and wrecked much of Kobe, killing more than 6,000 people.
India’s prime minister was shot by two of her Sikh bodyguards in the garden of her residence in New Delhi, months after the army stormed the Golden Temple.
General Niazi signed the surrender to Indian and Bangladeshi forces at the Ramna Race Course, ending the war in which Bangladesh won its independence.
Disguised as a soldier, the young Dalai Lama slipped out of the Norbulingka summer palace during the uprising against Chinese rule and escaped to India.
Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill met together for the first time, at the Soviet embassy in the Iranian capital, and agreed on the invasion of France.
Husayn ibn Ali, the Prophet’s grandson, was killed with his small band by an Umayyad army; Shia Muslims mourn him at Ashura, and his shrine stands at Karbala in Iraq.
An Israeli opponent of the Oslo peace accords shot the prime minister as he left a peace rally in Tel Aviv’s Kings of Israel Square, now Rabin Square.
Afonso de Albuquerque seized the sultanate’s trading city on the strait between Sumatra and the Malay peninsula, the gateway to the spice trade.
Perhaps the largest naval battle in history, fought around the Philippine island of Leyte, destroyed most of what was left of the Japanese navy; kamikazes were first used there.
Soldiers leapt from a truck during a military parade in Cairo and shot Egypt’s president, who had made peace with Israel, in the reviewing stand.
An American raid to seize militia leaders turned into an overnight street battle after two Black Hawk helicopters were shot down.

event: Lewis and Clark reach the Pacific
note: After 18 months crossing the continent, the expedition wintered at Fort Clatsop near the mouth of the Columbia River, in present-day Oregon.
Ulysses S. Grant starved out the Confederate fortress on the bluffs above the Mississippi after a 47-day siege, giving the Union control of the river.
William T. Sherman’s capture of the Confederate rail hub helped Lincoln win re-election; when he marched out in November, much of the city burned.
The abolitionist seized the federal armoury where the Shenandoah meets the Potomac, hoping to start a slave revolt; marines under Robert E. Lee captured him.
The first women’s rights convention, held in a chapel in upstate New York, demanded equal rights for women, including the vote.
A Tennessee teacher was tried for teaching evolution in the courthouse at Dayton; he was fined $100, but the clash of Darrow and Bryan gripped the country.
Frank Morris and the Anglin brothers left papier-mâché heads in their beds and paddled away from the island prison on a raft of raincoats; they were never found.
The tanker ran onto Bligh Reef in Prince William Sound, Alaska, and spilled some 40 million litres of crude oil along 2,000 km of coast.
Nine Black students needed paratroopers sent by President Eisenhower to escort them into Little Rock Central High School in Arkansas.
Four Black students sat down at the whites-only lunch counter of a Woolworth’s store in North Carolina and refused to leave; sit-ins spread across the South.

event: Cliff Palace is built at Mesa Verde
note: Ancestral Puebloans built the largest cliff dwelling in North America, about 150 rooms, under a sandstone overhang in south-west Colorado.
American troops stormed the hilltop castle guarding Mexico City; Mexico honours the young cadets who died defending it as the Niños Héroes.
A Portuguese fleet bound for India swung far west and sighted Monte Pascoal on the coast of Bahia, and Cabral claimed the land for Portugal.

event: The Graf Spee is scuttled off Montevideo
note: Cornered after a battle with three British cruisers, the German pocket battleship was blown up by her own crew in the estuary outside Montevideo.
A night-time clash between Chinese and Japanese troops at the old stone bridge south-west of Beijing escalated into full-scale war between the two countries.
At a vast ceremony on the plain north of Delhi, the king-emperor announced that India’s capital would move there from Calcutta.
Arab forces with T. E. Lawrence crossed the desert to take the Ottoman port at the head of the Red Sea from the landward side, where its guns could not reach.
Citizens of the South Korean city rose against martial law and held it for days before troops retook it; hundreds died.
Leaders of 29 newly independent Asian and African nations met in the Indonesian city and laid the foundations of the Non-Aligned Movement.
Napoleon landed with about a thousand men at Golfe-Juan on the Riviera and marched on Paris; within three weeks Louis XVIII had fled.

event: Napoleon dies in exile on St Helena
note: The fallen emperor spent his last six years at Longwood House on a remote British island in the South Atlantic.
Bosnian Serb forces in the surrounding hills besieged the city for nearly four years, the longest siege of a capital in modern warfare.
Twelve European countries signed the treaty in the Dutch city that created the European Union and set the path to the euro.

event: Reagan and Gorbachev meet in Reykjavík
note: In Höfði, a white wooden house by the sea, the two leaders came close to agreeing to scrap all nuclear weapons before the talks broke down over missile defence.
The Anglo-French supersonic airliner took off for the first time from Toulouse; it carried passengers at twice the speed of sound from 1976 until 2003.
The Queen and President Mitterrand opened the 50 km rail tunnel under the Strait of Dover between Folkestone and Coquelles.
Henry VIII watched from the shore as his warship heeled over and sank in the Solent while fighting a French fleet; she was raised in 1982.
In the US Army’s first major battle against the Germans, Rommel’s attack drove inexperienced American troops back through a gap in the mountains of western Tunisia.

event: Speke finds the source of the Nile
note: Speke reached the falls where the Nile leaves Lake Victoria, at what is now Jinja in Uganda; a dam drowned the falls in 1954.
The first mammal cloned from an adult cell was born at the Roslin Institute outside Edinburgh.
Working late in his laboratory at the University of Würzburg, the German physicist noticed a screen glowing across the room from a covered tube.
Two German hikers found the 5,300-year-old mummy melting out of a glacier in the Ötztal Alps on the Austrian–Italian border; he had been shot with an arrow.

event: The first public steam railway opens
note: George Stephenson’s Locomotion No. 1 hauled coal wagons and passengers between Shildon, Darlington and Stockton in north-east England.

event: The world’s first iron bridge opens
note: Abraham Darby III cast the 30 m arch over the River Severn in Shropshire, at the heart of the early Industrial Revolution.
Spencer Gore won the first lawn tennis championship, played at the All England Club’s ground off Worple Road before about 200 spectators.

event: The Rite of Spring causes a riot
note: Stravinsky’s ballet, with Nijinsky’s jerky choreography, provoked uproar on its first night at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris.

event: Fidel Castro attacks the Moncada Barracks
note: The failed attack on the army post in Santiago de Cuba landed Castro in prison and gave his later movement its name, the 26th of July.

event: Magellan finds a way through to the Pacific
note: Magellan’s ships spent 38 days threading the channels between Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego before entering the ocean he named the Pacific.

event: The Franklin expedition is lost in the Arctic
note: Sir John Franklin’s two ships were trapped in ice off King William Island while searching for the Northwest Passage; all 129 men died, and the wrecks were found in 2014 and 2016.
Soldiers opened fire on student protesters in the Plaza de las Tres Culturas in Mexico City ten days before the Olympics opened; hundreds may have died.
The murder of the popular Liberal leader Jorge Eliécer Gaitán in central Bogotá set off riots that destroyed much of the city and opened a decade of violence in Colombia.
Simón Bolívar’s victory on the plain south-west of Valencia secured Venezuela’s independence from Spain.
Princess Isabel signed the “Golden Law” at the imperial palace in Rio de Janeiro, freeing the last enslaved people in the Americas; the monarchy fell the next year.

event: The great stele of Axum is raised
note: The kings of Aksum raised giant carved granite stelae over their tombs in northern Ethiopia; Italy took one to Rome in 1937 and returned it in 2005.
British troops seized a hilltop in Natal at night, only to find at dawn that Boer guns overlooked them; they abandoned it after a day of slaughter.

event: The Great Mosque of Kairouan is founded
note: Uqba ibn Nafi founded the mosque when he built Kairouan as the Arab capital of North Africa; it became a model for mosques across the Maghreb.
The Fatimids built the mosque as the centre of their new capital, and its teaching made it one of the oldest and most famous seats of learning in the Islamic world.
The Mamluk sultan tricked the Knights Hospitaller into surrendering the great crusader castle in western Syria with a forged letter after a month’s siege.
Tokugawa Ieyasu destroyed the Toyotomi clan by taking Osaka Castle, ending the last challenge to the Tokugawa shogunate.
Betrayed by his general Akechi Mitsuhide, the warlord who had almost united Japan died in the burning temple in Kyoto.

event: The Battle of the Chosin Reservoir
note: US Marines and allied troops, surrounded by Chinese armies in temperatures of –30 °C, fought their way out to the coast of North Korea.
Japan’s five-month siege of the Russian naval base at the tip of the Liaodong Peninsula cost tens of thousands of lives in assaults on its hill forts.

event: The ironclads Monitor and Merrimack clash
note: The first battle between armoured warships, off Norfolk, Virginia, ended in a draw, and every wooden navy in the world was suddenly obsolete.
Wellington’s allied army and Blücher’s Prussians defeated Napoleon on the ridges about 15 km south of Brussels, ending the Hundred Days. The Lion’s Mound now marks the field.

event: Christopher Columbus makes landfall in the Americas
note: Columbus’s first landfall was an island the Lucayans called Guanahani. Most historians identify it with San Salvador in the Bahamas, though Samana Cay and others have been proposed.
Athenian and Plataean hoplites routed a Persian landing force on the coastal plain of Marathon, north-east of Athens; the 192 Athenian dead were buried in the mound that still stands on the field.
Henry V’s outnumbered and largely archer army defeated the French nobility on muddy fields between the woods of Azincourt and Tramecourt in northern France.
Nelson’s fleet destroyed the combined French and Spanish fleets off Cape Trafalgar in south-west Spain, ending Napoleon’s hopes of invading Britain; Nelson was killed by a French marksman.

event: The Battle of the Little Bighorn
note: Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors wiped out Custer’s battalion of the 7th Cavalry on the ridges above the Little Bighorn River in Montana.
The north face of the volcano in Washington State collapsed in the largest landslide ever recorded, unleashing a sideways blast that flattened 600 km² of forest; 57 people died.

event: French soldiers find the Rosetta Stone
note: Troops rebuilding a fort near the Nile port of Rashid (Rosetta) found the stone, whose decree in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek became the key to reading hieroglyphs.
A German torpedo sank the Cunard liner off the Old Head of Kinsale in southern Ireland; 1,198 people died, 128 of them Americans, hardening US opinion against Germany.

event: Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin meet at Yalta
note: The Allied leaders met at the tsars’ former summer palace of Livadia in Crimea to plan the defeat of Germany and the shape of post-war Europe.

event: Joan of Arc is burned at the stake
note: Captured by the Burgundians and convicted of heresy by a pro-English church court, Joan was burned in the old market square of Rouen, aged about 19.

event: Samuel de Champlain founds a settlement on the St Lawrence
note: Champlain built his ‘Habitation’ below the cliffs where the St Lawrence narrows, founding Quebec, the first permanent settlement of New France.
On the banks of the Ipiranga brook, then just outside São Paulo, the Portuguese prince regent cried ‘Independence or death!’ and became Brazil’s first emperor.
About 1,400 CIA-trained Cuban exiles landed on Cuba’s south coast; Castro’s forces defeated them around Playa Girón within three days.

event: Shipyard strikers win the right to found Solidarity
note: A strike at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk, led by the electrician Lech Wałęsa, won the right to form Solidarity, the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc.
The Duke of Cumberland’s army crushed Charles Edward Stuart’s Jacobites on Drummossie Moor east of Inverness in under an hour: the last pitched battle on British soil.

event: Chile’s presidential palace is bombed in Pinochet’s coup
note: Air force jets rocketed La Moneda palace in central Santiago as the armed forces seized power; President Salvador Allende died inside, and General Pinochet ruled for 17 years.
Napoleon lured the Russian and Austrian emperors into attacking his weakened right, then seized the Pratzen Heights at the centre of their line, east of Brno in Moravia.

The longest battle of the First World War was fought around the forts north of Verdun; about 300,000 French and German soldiers died. The Douaumont ossuary holds the bones of 130,000 unidentified men.

event: The Second Battle of El Alamein
note: Montgomery’s Eighth Army broke through Rommel’s lines between the coast and the Qattara Depression, about 100 km west of Alexandria, turning the war in North Africa.
US carrier aircraft sank four Japanese carriers north-west of Midway Atoll, a remote US base about 2,100 km from Hawaii, turning the tide of the Pacific war.

event: US Marines raise the flag over Iwo Jima
note: Joe Rosenthal’s photograph of Marines raising the flag on Mount Suribachi, the volcanic island’s highest point, became the most reproduced image of the war; the battle lasted five weeks.

event: The Battle of Dien Bien Phu
note: The Viet Minh hauled artillery onto the hills around a French fortified valley in north-west Vietnam and forced its surrender, ending French rule in Indochina.

event: James Cook’s Endeavour lands at Botany Bay
note: Cook anchored in a bay he named for the plants his naturalists collected there; the landing at Kurnell was the first British contact with Aboriginal people on Australia’s east coast.

event: The Treaty of Waitangi is signed
note: More than 40 Māori chiefs signed the treaty with the British Crown on the lawn at Waitangi in the Bay of Islands; its English and Māori texts differ, and it remains New Zealand’s founding document.

event: German and Italian aircraft bomb Guernica
note: Planes supporting Franco bombed the Basque market town for three hours; Picasso’s painting made it a lasting symbol of the horror of war.
Trapped on the York River peninsula in Virginia by Washington’s army and a French fleet, Cornwallis surrendered, effectively ending the American War of Independence.

event: The Romans take the fortress of Masada
note: The Tenth Legion built a huge ramp up the desert mesa above the Dead Sea to take Herod’s fortress; according to Josephus, its Jewish defenders chose death over capture.
A pyroclastic flow engulfed Saint-Pierre, then the largest town in Martinique, killing about 28,000 people; a prisoner in a thick-walled cell was among the few survivors.

event: British and French troops burn the Old Summer Palace
note: At the end of the Second Opium War, troops looted and then burned the emperors’ vast gardens of Yuanmingyuan, north-west of Beijing, in reprisal for the torture of envoys.

event: Thomas Becket is murdered in his cathedral
note: Four knights who took Henry II’s angry words as an order killed the archbishop in Canterbury Cathedral; he was made a saint within three years.

event: Bedouin shepherds find the Dead Sea Scrolls
note: The first scrolls came from caves near Qumran, above the north-west shore of the Dead Sea; they include the oldest known manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible.

event: The Korean War armistice is signed
note: The armistice was signed at Panmunjom on the front line near the 38th parallel; no peace treaty followed, and the demilitarised zone still divides Korea.

event: The last Muslim kingdom in Spain surrenders
note: Muhammad XII (Boabdil) handed the Alhambra and the city of Granada to Ferdinand and Isabella, ending almost eight centuries of Muslim rule in Iberia.

event: Gandhi’s Salt March reaches the sea
note: After 24 days and about 390 km on foot, Gandhi reached the coastal village of Dandi in Gujarat and picked up a lump of natural salt in defiance of the British salt tax.

Troops under Brigadier-General Dyer fired without warning on a crowd in the walled Jallianwala Bagh garden near the Golden Temple, killing at least 379 people by the official count, many more by others.
The Virginia Company’s settlers built a fort on a marshy island in the James River: the first permanent English settlement in the Americas, where most died in the first years.
Alexander died aged 32 in Nebuchadnezzar’s palace at Babylon, on the Euphrates south of modern Baghdad, after a sudden fever; his empire soon split among his generals.

event: Christiaan Barnard performs the first human heart transplant
note: Barnard’s team at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town gave Louis Washkansky the heart of a young road-accident victim; he lived for 18 days.
After a three-year siege, Scipio Aemilianus’s army stormed and razed the city near modern Tunis, ending the Third Punic War; Rome later refounded it as a colony.
English longbowmen under Edward III cut down wave after wave of French knights on a hillside in Picardy, early in the Hundred Years’ War.
Cromwell’s cavalry and the New Model Army crushed Charles I’s main army in Northamptonshire, deciding the English Civil War.
The Swedish king was killed leading a cavalry charge in fog south-west of Leipzig, although his army won the battle.
British, French and Russian ships destroyed an Ottoman–Egyptian fleet in the bay of Navarino in the Peloponnese, the last great battle of sailing ships, securing Greek independence.
After a year’s siege, the starving Greek defenders of the lagoon town tried to break out at night; most were killed, and the town became a symbol of the war, where Byron had died in 1824.
British, French and Ottoman armies besieged Russia’s Black Sea naval base in the Crimea for eleven months before the Russians abandoned it.
Hindenburg and Ludendorff encircled and destroyed a Russian army in the forests and lakes of East Prussia, now northern Poland.
Józef Piłsudski’s counter-attack threw back the Red Army at the gates of Warsaw, saving the new Polish state.

event: Three children see the Virgin at Fátima
note: Three shepherd children said a lady appeared to them in a field in central Portugal; the sanctuary built there draws millions of pilgrims.

event: The first Geneva Convention is signed
note: Twelve states agreed in Geneva’s town hall to protect wounded soldiers and the medics who treat them, under the sign of a red cross.
Chieftains gathered each summer at Þingvellir, in a rift valley east of Reykjavík, for one of the oldest parliaments in the world.
King Olaf Haraldsson was killed fighting a peasant army near Trondheim; within a year he was hailed as a saint, the patron of Norway.
Queen Margaret had her great-nephew Eric crowned king of Denmark, Norway and Sweden at Kalmar castle, uniting the three kingdoms under one crown.

event: Emperor Henry IV kneels at Canossa
note: Excommunicated by Pope Gregory VII, the emperor waited three days in the snow outside the castle of Canossa in the Apennines before the pope lifted the ban.

event: The Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa
note: The kings of Castile, Aragon and Navarre crushed the Almohad caliph’s army in the Sierra Morena, opening southern Spain to Christian conquest.
A colliery spoil tip slid down a hillside in a Welsh mining village and buried the primary school; 116 children and 28 adults died.
Mostly Canadian troops landed on the beaches of the French port in a disastrous trial raid; more than half of them were killed, wounded or captured.
The landings south of Rome were meant to outflank the German line at Cassino, but the beachhead was penned in for four months.
An explosion at a chemical plant north of Milan released a cloud of dioxin over nearby towns, leading to new European rules on industrial safety.
The plane carrying Manchester United’s “Busby Babes” home from Belgrade crashed in slush on its third take-off attempt from Munich-Riem airport; 23 people died.

event: The sinking of the Wilhelm Gustloff
note: A Soviet submarine torpedoed the overcrowded German liner evacuating refugees in the Baltic off Pomerania; over 9,000 people died, the worst loss of life in a single sinking.
Parisians who refused to give up the National Guard’s cannon on Montmartre took over the city for two months, until government troops crushed them in the Bloody Week.
The French revolutionary army held its ground against the Prussians near a windmill in the Champagne, and the republic was proclaimed the next day.

event: The siege of the Alcázar of Toledo
note: Nationalist troops and civilians held out in the fortress above Toledo for 70 days until Franco’s army relieved them.
A storm surge broke the dykes of Zeeland, in the south-west Netherlands, drowning over 1,800 people and prompting the Delta Works.
Five countries signed it aboard a riverboat on the Moselle at the Luxembourg village where France, Germany and Luxembourg meet.

event: Hitler announces the Anschluss in Vienna
note: Days after German troops crossed the border, Hitler told a huge crowd on the Heldenplatz that his homeland Austria had joined the German Reich.
The Soviet secret police shot some 22,000 Polish officers and other prisoners, many of them buried in the Katyn forest near Smolensk.
Russian sappers blew a breach in the walls of the Tatar khanate’s capital on the Volga, opening the way east to Siberia.

event: The Lion Gate is built at Mycenae
note: Two carved lionesses guard the main entrance to the citadel of Mycenae, the city Homer made the home of Agamemnon.

event: Philip of Macedon wins at Chaeronea
note: Philip and his teenage son Alexander defeated Athens and Thebes in Boeotia, making Macedon the master of Greece.
Kemal (later Atatürk) landed at the Black Sea port to organise resistance to the Allied occupation, the start of the Turkish War of Independence.
A riot at the hour of vespers outside a church in Palermo turned into a massacre of the French, and Sicily threw off the rule of Charles of Anjou.

event: The last emperor of the West is deposed
note: The Germanic general Odoacer deposed the boy emperor at Ravenna, the western capital, a date often used for the fall of the Roman Empire in the West.
A gang stopped the Glasgow–London mail train at a bridge in Buckinghamshire and stole £2.6 million in used banknotes.
High King Brian Boru broke the power of the Vikings of Dublin and their allies on the shore north of the city but was killed in his tent.

event: William Wallace wins at Stirling Bridge
note: Wallace and Andrew Moray let the English army cross the narrow bridge over the Forth, then attacked before the rest could follow.
Napoleon beat the Austrians on the Marchfeld plain north-east of Vienna in one of the largest battles of the age.
The British Residency in Lucknow held out for almost five months during the Indian Rebellion before relief columns broke through.
At a meeting at Gowalia Tank maidan in Bombay, Gandhi told India to “do or die”; he and the Congress leaders were arrested the next morning.
The Muslim League, meeting in a Lahore park, called for independent states for India’s Muslims; Minar-e-Pakistan now marks the spot.

event: Ashoka builds the Great Stupa at Sanchi
note: The emperor’s brick stupa on a hill in central India was later enlarged and given four carved stone gateways, among the finest early Buddhist art.

event: The Kailasa temple is carved at Ellora
note: Rashtrakuta kings had a whole temple carved down into a basalt hillside in Maharashtra, removing an estimated 200,000 tonnes of rock.
Afonso de Albuquerque took the island city from the Sultan of Bijapur, and it remained the capital of Portuguese India for 450 years.
A British-Indian army and its camp followers, some 16,000 people, were destroyed in the snowbound passes; the last stand was at Gandamak.

event: Soviet commandos storm the Tajbeg Palace
note: Special forces killed Afghanistan’s president Hafizullah Amin in his palace outside Kabul, starting the Soviet war in Afghanistan.

event: Students seize the US embassy in Tehran
note: Iranian students took 52 American diplomats and citizens hostage and held them for 444 days.
The Assyrian king collected thousands of clay tablets, including the Epic of Gilgamesh, in his palace at Nineveh, across the Tigris from modern Mosul.

event: The Great Altar of Pergamon is built
note: King Eumenes II built the altar, carved with a battle of gods and giants, on the acropolis of Pergamon; it now stands in a Berlin museum.
Caliph al-Walid I built one of the oldest and grandest mosques in the world on the site of a Christian basilica in the heart of Damascus.
Muhammad’s followers dug a ditch across the open northern side of Medina, and a Meccan coalition army gave up its siege after a month.
The Mongol capital in the Orkhon valley drew envoys, merchants and craftsmen from across Eurasia; a silver fountain in its palace poured four drinks.

event: Lin Zexu destroys the opium at Humen
note: The imperial commissioner had over 1,000 tonnes of seized British opium mixed with lime and salt and flushed into the Pearl River, triggering the First Opium War.

event: Chiang Kai-shek is kidnapped at Xi’an
note: Two of his own generals seized the Nationalist leader at the hot springs outside Xi’an to force him into an alliance with the Communists against Japan.
The first great battle of the war between China and Japan lasted three months in and around the city; the last defenders held out in a warehouse by Suzhou Creek.
The Ming loyalist general besieged the Dutch fort for nine months and ended Dutch rule on Taiwan.

event: The Great Buddha of Kamakura is cast
note: The 13 m bronze Buddha once sat inside a temple hall, which was washed away by a tsunami in 1498; it has sat in the open air ever since.

event: The Dutch are moved to Dejima
note: For two centuries a small artificial island in Nagasaki harbour was Japan’s only window on the West, where Dutch traders were allowed to live.

event: Korea’s queen is murdered in her palace
note: Japanese agents broke into Gyeongbokgung Palace in Seoul and killed Queen Min, who had resisted Japanese influence, and burned her body.
North Vietnamese divisions surrounded the US Marine base near the Laotian border for 77 days under some of the heaviest bombing of the war.
A month of street fighting to retake the Philippine capital from the Japanese destroyed much of the old walled city and killed some 100,000 civilians.

event: The Soviet Union tests its first atomic bomb
note: The bomb, nicknamed “First Lightning”, was exploded on a tower on the steppe of the Semipalatinsk test site in Kazakhstan, four years after Hiroshima.
A shallow earthquake directly beneath the Uzbek capital destroyed much of the old city and left 300,000 people homeless.
Persian troops with English ships took the Portuguese fortress on the island at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, ending a century of Portuguese control of its trade.
King Herod built a port city with an artificial harbour on the coast of Judea and named it after Augustus; it became the Roman capital of the province.

event: The Temple of Jupiter rises at Baalbek
note: The Romans built one of their largest temples in the Beqaa Valley of Lebanon on a platform of stones weighing up to 800 tonnes.

event: The siege of the Beijing legations
note: Boxer fighters and Qing troops besieged foreign diplomats and Chinese Christians in the legation quarter for 55 days until an eight-nation army arrived.

event: The Dunhuang library cave is opened
note: A Taoist monk found a walled-up cave in the Mogao Caves on the Silk Road holding tens of thousands of manuscripts, including the oldest dated printed book.
Samurai assassins killed Ii Naosuke, the shogun’s chief minister who had signed treaties with the West, outside a gate of Edo Castle.
Boer forces besieged the Natal town and its British garrison for 118 days until Redvers Buller’s relief force broke through after repeated failures.
