A British square armed with Gatling guns broke the Zulu army in front of King Cetshwayo’s royal kraal, ending the Anglo-Zulu War.
The Scottish explorer became the first European known to see the Niger, “glittering to the morning sun” at Ségou in present-day Mali, and found that it flowed east.

event: Timbuktu’s Sankoré mosque becomes a seat of learning
note: Scholars at the mud-brick mosque taught law, astronomy and medicine; families in the city still keep thousands of old manuscripts.

event: The War of the Golden Stool
note: When the British governor demanded to sit on the sacred Golden Stool of the Asante, Queen Mother Yaa Asantewaa led a rising and besieged the British fort in Kumasi.
At the handover ceremony in Léopoldville, now Kinshasa, the Congo’s new prime minister answered the Belgian king with a fierce attack on colonial rule; he was murdered seven months later.
The fort guarding the old harbour of Mombasa in Kenya changed hands nine times between Portugal, Oman and Mombasa’s own rulers.

event: Fasilides builds his castle at Gondar
note: The Ethiopian emperor founded a permanent capital north of Lake Tana, where his successors added castles to a walled royal enclosure.
The emperor born in the city lavished buildings on it, including a four-way triumphal arch; its ruins on the Libyan coast are among the finest in the Roman world.
French paratroopers broke the independence fighters’ network in the Casbah, using torture that later caused outrage in France.
Rif fighters under Abd el-Krim routed a Spanish army in north-east Morocco; some 8,000 Spanish soldiers died.
Settlers sent by Cecil Rhodes’s company raised the Union Jack at Fort Salisbury, now Harare, the start of colonial Rhodesia.
German troops drove the Herero into the Omaheke desert of Namibia, where most of them died; Germany has since called it a genocide.

event: Cape Coast Castle becomes Britain’s Gold Coast headquarters
note: Enslaved Africans were held in its dungeons before being shipped across the Atlantic; it stands 15 km east of Elmina on the coast of Ghana.
Egypt’s ruler invited the Mamluk beys to a ceremony at the Cairo Citadel and had them shot down in a narrow passage, ending their power.

event: Usman dan Fodio founds the Sokoto Caliphate
note: The Fulani scholar’s holy war united the Hausa city-states into one of the largest states in 19th-century Africa, ruled from Sokoto in north-west Nigeria.

event: Black Loyalists from Nova Scotia found Freetown
note: Some 1,100 freed African Americans who had fought for Britain sailed from Canada and founded Freetown, the capital of Sierra Leone, beside a great cotton tree.

event: The Great Mosque of Kilwa is built
note: The coral-stone mosque on an island off southern Tanzania served Kilwa, a Swahili city grown rich on the gold trade from the interior.
At noon a gunshot sent some 50,000 settlers racing to claim plots of former Indian Territory; Oklahoma City had 10,000 people by nightfall.
A bomb thrown at police breaking up a labour rally in Chicago killed seven officers; the rally’s cause, the eight-hour day, is remembered on 1 May.
An earth dam holding a wealthy club’s lake burst upstream of the Pennsylvania steel town, and the wall of water killed over 2,200 people.
White mobs burned Greenwood, Tulsa’s prosperous Black district known as Black Wall Street, killing as many as 300 people.

event: The first nuclear reactor goes critical
note: Enrico Fermi’s team started the first self-sustaining chain reaction in a pile of graphite bricks under the stands of a football field at the University of Chicago.
The French flag was lowered at the Cabildo in New Orleans, and the United States doubled in size for $15 million.
Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded the oldest continuously settled European city in the United States on Florida’s Atlantic coast.
American businessmen, backed by US Marines, forced Queen Liliʻuokalani from power at ʻIolani Palace in Honolulu.
Delegates who had come to discuss a union of the Maritime colonies began planning Canadian Confederation on Prince Edward Island instead.

event: The last spike of the Canadian Pacific Railway
note: Donald Smith drove a plain iron spike at Craigellachie in the Monashee Mountains of British Columbia, linking Canada by rail from coast to coast.
Canadian troops overran the Métis capital on the South Saskatchewan River, ending the North-West Rebellion; Louis Riel surrendered and was hanged.
Nadia Comăneci scored the first perfect 10 in gymnastics; the stadium’s tilted tower was not finished until 1987, and its debt took 30 years to pay off.

event: Pancho Villa raids Columbus, New Mexico
note: Villa’s Mexican revolutionaries attacked the border town and its army camp, and the United States sent General Pershing into Mexico after him.
The surrender of a whole British army in upstate New York persuaded France to enter the war on the American side.
A Confederate surprise attack on Grant’s camps by the Tennessee River led to two days of fighting with more casualties than all America’s earlier wars combined.

event: Washington’s army winters at Valley Forge
note: Some 2,000 soldiers died of disease in the camp north-west of Philadelphia, but the army that marched out had been drilled into shape by Baron von Steuben.
After crossing the icy river on Christmas night, Washington’s troops surprised the Hessian garrison of Trenton, New Jersey.
The Italian liner was rammed in fog by the Swedish ship Stockholm off Nantucket; rescuers saved over 1,600 people before she sank.

event: The Hieroglyphic Stairway is built at Copán
note: The Maya city in western Honduras recorded its dynasty’s history in some 2,200 glyphs carved on the 62 steps of a temple stairway.
The Inca emperor’s army besieged the Spanish in the old capital for ten months; the fiercest fighting was for the fortress of Sacsayhuamán above the city.

event: The Battle of Cartagena de Indias
note: A huge British fleet under Edward Vernon failed to take Spain’s fortified Caribbean port in Colombia, defended by the one-legged Blas de Lezo.
The Welsh privateer crossed the isthmus and looted Panama City, which burned; the Spanish rebuilt it a few kilometres away.
Scotland’s attempt to found a trading colony on the Isthmus of Panama ended in disease and ruin, and helped push Scotland into union with England.
A British expedition took Spain’s great Caribbean port after a two-month siege, then handed it back the next year in exchange for Florida.
Jean-Jacques Dessalines proclaimed the first Black republic at Gonaïves, after formerly enslaved people had defeated Napoleon’s army.
After crossing the Andes from Argentina, José de San Martín’s army defeated the Spanish north of Santiago, freeing central Chile.
The Chilean corvette Esmeralda fought the Peruvian ironclad Huáscar off the nitrate port until she was rammed and sunk with her flag still flying.
The earthquakes wrecked the colonial capital of Central America, and the government moved to the site of the present Guatemala City.
The earthquake struck beneath Nicaragua’s capital just after midnight, killing about 10,000 people; aid stolen by the Somoza regime fuelled the revolution.

event: Archbishop Óscar Romero is shot at Mass
note: A gunman shot the Archbishop of San Salvador as he celebrated Mass in a hospital chapel, a day after he had told soldiers to stop the killing.

event: Fidel Castro lands from the Granma
note: Eighty-two rebels sailed from Mexico in an overloaded yacht and ran aground in a mangrove swamp in eastern Cuba; only about 20 reached the Sierra Maestra.
The earthquake began off the Pacific coast, but the old lake bed under the capital amplified the shaking, and thousands died in collapsed buildings there.

event: Bolívar meets San Martín at Guayaquil
note: The two liberators met privately in the Ecuadorian port; afterwards San Martín withdrew from public life and left Bolívar to finish freeing Peru.
The Dutch navigator anchored in Golden Bay at the top of the South Island, where a clash with Māori canoes left four of his men dead; he never landed.
New Zealand’s deadliest earthquake levelled Napier and Hastings; the town was rebuilt in Art Deco style on land that had risen by up to 2.7 m.
A sightseeing DC-10 flew into the slopes of the Antarctic volcano in a whiteout, killing all 257 people aboard.

event: Canberra is founded as Australia’s capital
note: Lady Denman named the purpose-built capital at a ceremony in a sheep paddock between Sydney and Melbourne, which had both wanted the honour.
The Dutch East India ship struck a reef off Western Australia; mutineers on the islands murdered over 100 survivors before rescue came.
Edward Hargraves, back from California, washed gold out of a creek near Bathurst in New South Wales and set off Australia’s gold rushes.
American forces took the island in the Marianas, putting Tokyo within range of B-29 bombers; hundreds of civilians jumped from the northern cliffs rather than surrender.

event: Cook observes the transit of Venus
note: James Cook and the astronomer Charles Green timed the planet’s passage across the Sun from Point Venus on Tahiti, to help measure the distance to the Sun.

event: Kamehameha wins the Battle of Nuʻuanu
note: Kamehameha’s army drove the defenders of Oʻahu up the Nuʻuanu valley above Honolulu and over the cliffs of the Pali, bringing most of Hawaii under his rule.
The British Expeditionary Force fought its first battle of the war along a canal in Belgium before retreating; a legend grew that angels had protected it.

event: The First Battle of the Marne
note: French and British armies stopped the German advance east of Paris, helped by troops rushed to the front in Paris taxis.
German troops released chlorine gas from cylinders against French colonial troops north of Ypres, the first large gas attack on the Western Front.
German and Austrian troops broke through the Italian line in the Julian Alps, now in Slovenia, and drove the Italians back over 100 km.
Some 400 British tanks punched through the German line south-west of Cambrai in the first mass tank attack, but most of the ground was soon lost.
Revolutionaries led by the schoolteacher Surya Sen seized the police armoury in the Bengal port city to strike at British rule.
China signed away Taiwan and recognised Korea’s independence at a restaurant in the Japanese port, ending the First Sino-Japanese War.
The stone houses of a Neolithic village on Orkney, complete with stone beds and dressers, were uncovered by a storm in 1850.
At the winter solstice, sunrise shines down the passage into the chamber of the great tomb mound in Ireland’s Boyne Valley, which is older than the pyramids.

event: The stones of Carnac are raised
note: Neolithic people set up more than 3,000 standing stones in long rows near the coast of Brittany.

event: Croesus consults the oracle at Delphi
note: Told that if he attacked Persia he would destroy a great empire, the king of Lydia attacked and destroyed his own; Apollo’s priestess spoke at his temple on Mount Parnassus.

event: The theatre of Epidaurus is built
note: The theatre at the healing sanctuary of Asclepius seats 14,000, and its acoustics carry a whisper on stage to the back row.
The great white stupa at Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka’s ancient capital, is said to enshrine relics of the Buddha.

event: Kush buries its kings at Meroë
note: The kings and queens of Kush were buried under some 200 small, steep pyramids in the desert by the Nile in Sudan.
The charter was agreed at Runnymede, a Thames-side meadow between Windsor and Staines where the rebel barons met the king on neutral ground. The exact spot is unknown.
Hannibal’s outnumbered army enveloped and destroyed eight Roman legions on the plain of the Aufidus (Ofanto) in Apulia, one of the bloodiest days in history; the exact field is debated.
Octavian’s fleet under Agrippa defeated Antony and Cleopatra off the mouth of the Ambracian Gulf in western Greece; their flight to Egypt left Octavian master of the Roman world.
Themistocles lured Xerxes’ larger fleet into the narrow channel between the island of Salamis and the coast of Attica, where the Greek triremes routed it.

The galleys of the Holy League under Don John of Austria destroyed the Ottoman fleet off the Echinades islands at the mouth of the Gulf of Patras; Cervantes lost the use of his left hand in the fight.

event: The Charge of the Light Brigade
note: Through a misunderstood order, about 670 British light cavalry charged Russian guns down the North Valley near Balaklava in Crimea; nearly half were killed, wounded or captured.
William III defeated James II at a ford of the River Boyne near Drogheda, securing the Protestant succession; Ulster’s Orangemen still mark it each July.
Charles Martel’s Franks stopped an Umayyad army somewhere between Poitiers and Tours, traditionally at Moussais-la-Bataille; the exact site, and even the year, are disputed.

event: The Black Death reaches Sicily aboard Genoese galleys
note: Ships from the Black Sea brought plague into the harbour of Messina; within four years the Black Death had killed perhaps a third of Europe’s people.

event: Gold is found at Sutter’s Mill
note: James Marshall spotted gold flakes in the tailrace of a sawmill he was building for John Sutter on the South Fork of the American River, setting off the California Gold Rush.
Soviet tank armies clashed head-on with the II SS Panzer Corps near the village of Prokhorovka at the height of the Battle of Kursk, among the largest tank battles in history.
US Marines landed at Wolmido island and the port of Incheon, far behind North Korean lines and despite huge tides; Seoul was retaken within two weeks.
Tokugawa Ieyasu’s victory in a mountain valley in central Japan, helped by defections from the enemy army, opened 250 years of rule by the Tokugawa shoguns.

event: Commodore Perry’s black ships arrive in Japan
note: Perry’s four warships anchored off Uraga at the mouth of Edo Bay and demanded that Japan open its ports, ending more than two centuries of seclusion.
Police opened fire on a crowd protesting the pass laws outside the police station in Sharpeville township, south of Johannesburg, killing 69 people.
Police fired on schoolchildren marching against compulsory teaching in Afrikaans; 12-year-old Hector Pieterson became the symbol of a rising that spread across South Africa.
The Ottomans under Murad I fought a Serbian-led army on the Field of Blackbirds, just north-west of Pristina; both rulers were killed, and the battle became central to Serbian national memory.
After an eight-month search, the journalist Henry Morton Stanley found the missionary at Ujiji on Lake Tanganyika and greeted him, he later claimed, with ‘Dr Livingstone, I presume?’

event: Marconi receives the first transatlantic radio signal
note: Guglielmo Marconi heard the Morse letter ‘S’, sent from Poldhu in Cornwall, on a receiver at Signal Hill above St John’s, Newfoundland, its aerial held aloft by a kite.

event: The golden spike completes the first transcontinental railroad
note: Leland Stanford drove a ceremonial golden spike where the Central Pacific and Union Pacific lines met at Promontory Summit in Utah.

The British drove the colonial militia from Breed’s Hill on the Charlestown peninsula, across the river from Boston, at a cost of more than 1,000 casualties; the battle took its name from neighbouring Bunker Hill.
A Zulu army of some 20,000 overwhelmed a British camp beneath the sphinx-shaped hill of Isandlwana, the worst defeat of a British army by an indigenous force.
Cook was killed in a skirmish on the shore of Kealakekua Bay, on the Kona coast of Hawaii’s Big Island, after trying to take a chief hostage over a stolen boat.
Napoleon’s bloodiest battle was fought about 120 km west of Moscow; the Russians withdrew after losing some 45,000 men, and Napoleon entered Moscow a week later.

event: Argentina surrenders, ending the Falklands War
note: Once British troops had taken the mountains ringing the islands’ capital, the Argentine commander surrendered his garrison of about 9,800 men at Stanley.

The bloodiest single day in American history: some 23,000 casualties near Sharpsburg, Maryland, as McClellan checked Lee’s first invasion of the North, giving Lincoln his opening to announce emancipation.

event: The emperor Akbar founds Fatehpur Sikri
note: Akbar built a new red-sandstone capital at Sikri, west of Agra, honouring a Sufi saint who had foretold the birth of his son; it was largely abandoned after about 14 years.

event: Mexico defeats the French at Puebla
note: General Ignacio Zaragoza’s army repelled a French assault on the hill forts of Loreto and Guadalupe above Puebla, a victory remembered as Cinco de Mayo; the French took the city a year later.

event: Sepoys mutiny, sparking the Indian Rebellion
note: Sepoys at the Meerut cantonment, north-east of Delhi, rose after comrades were jailed for refusing cartridges rumoured to be greased with animal fat, then marched on Delhi.

event: China signs the treaty ending the First Opium War
note: The treaty was signed aboard HMS Cornwallis on the Yangtze at Nanjing; China ceded Hong Kong Island and opened five ports to British trade.

event: Operation Market Garden fails at the ‘bridge too far’
note: Allied airborne troops tried to seize a chain of Dutch bridges; British paratroops held the north end of the Rhine bridge at Arnhem for four days before being overwhelmed.

event: Vikings raid the monastery on Lindisfarne
note: Norse raiders sacked the monastery on Holy Island off the Northumbrian coast, an attack usually taken as the start of the Viking Age in Britain.

event: Norse explorers camp in North America
note: The only confirmed Norse site in the Americas lies at the northern tip of Newfoundland; tree rings show the Vikings were cutting wood there in 1021.

event: Great Zimbabwe rises in southern Africa
note: The stone city near modern Masvingo was the capital of a kingdom that traded gold and ivory to the Swahili coast; its Great Enclosure is the largest ancient structure south of the Sahara.

event: The Maya build El Castillo at Chichén Itzá
note: The stepped temple to the feathered serpent Kukulcán stands in the Yucatán; at the equinoxes, the light makes a shadow serpent crawl down its northern stair.
The Nazca people scraped hundreds of lines and giant animal figures into the desert plateau of southern Peru, between the towns of Nazca and Palpa; they are best seen from the air.
Emperor Constantine summoned the first ecumenical council of bishops to Nicaea (modern İznik), south-east of Constantinople; it produced the Nicene Creed.
US Marines seized the airfield the Japanese were building on Guadalcanal in the Solomon Islands; six months of fighting on land and sea ended with Japan’s withdrawal.
Carrier aircraft from the force that had struck Pearl Harbor bombed the port of Darwin, the first and heaviest of almost 100 air raids on northern Australia.
Kitchener’s Anglo-Egyptian army, armed with Maxim guns, destroyed the Mahdist army on the plain north of Omdurman, opposite Khartoum; the young Winston Churchill rode in the cavalry charge.

event: The Black Prince captures the French king at Poitiers
note: Edward the Black Prince’s outnumbered army routed the French south-east of Poitiers and took King John II prisoner.
Philip II of France beat the emperor, King John’s allies and the Count of Flanders south-east of Lille; John’s failure led on to Magna Carta.
The infantry of the Lombard cities, rallied round their sacred carroccio wagon, defeated Emperor Frederick Barbarossa’s knights north-west of Milan.
On one day Napoleon beat one Prussian army on the plateau above Jena and Davout another at Auerstedt; Prussia collapsed within weeks.

event: Nelson turns a blind eye at Copenhagen
note: Ordered to break off, Nelson put his telescope to his blind eye, said he saw no signal, and went on to defeat the Danish fleet moored off the city.
Catholic imperial troops routed the Bohemian Protestants on a low hill west of Prague in under two hours, early in the Thirty Years’ War.
The Swedish king’s flexible brigades and light guns beat Tilly’s imperial army north of Leipzig, the first great Protestant victory of the Thirty Years’ War.
The 21-year-old Duc d’Enghien destroyed the famed Spanish infantry squares near the Belgian border, ending a century of Spanish military dominance.

event: Francis I is captured at Pavia
note: Imperial arquebusiers shot down the French cavalry in the hunting park north of Pavia and captured the French king, who wrote that all was lost save honour.

event: The Mongols destroy the Hungarian army at Mohi
note: Batu Khan and Subutai surrounded King Béla IV’s camp by the Sajó river and slaughtered much of the Hungarian nobility.
Two days before Mohi, a Mongol force defeated the knights of Duke Henry the Pious in Silesia and paraded his head on a spear.

event: The Crusade of Varna is destroyed
note: Sultan Murad II’s army defeated the last great crusade near the Black Sea port; the young King Władysław III of Poland and Hungary was killed.
Sultan Bayezid I crushed a crusader army of French and Hungarian knights on the Danube in what is now Bulgaria.
John Hunyadi broke Mehmed II’s siege of the fortress where the Sava meets the Danube; church bells ring at noon in its memory.
After six months, Suleiman the Magnificent let the Knights of St John leave the island with honour; they later settled on Malta.
The Venetian garrison of the Cypriot port held out for eleven months; after the surrender its commander, Marco Antonio Bragadin, was flayed alive.

event: Russia burns the Ottoman fleet at Chesma
note: Russian fireships destroyed almost the whole Ottoman fleet crammed into the bay of Çeşme on the Aegean coast of Anatolia.
Russian ships firing explosive shells destroyed an Ottoman squadron in the Black Sea harbour, helping draw Britain and France into the Crimean War.
Osman Pasha’s Ottoman army held the Bulgarian town against Russian and Romanian assaults for five months before trying to break out.

event: The defence of the Shipka Pass
note: Russian troops and Bulgarian volunteers held the pass through the Balkan Mountains against Ottoman attacks; a monument now crowns the peak.
The Prussians trapped the French army against the Belgian border and captured the emperor himself; Paris declared a republic two days later.
Prussian troops stormed the Danish redoubts in southern Jutland, deciding the war over Schleswig.
Cromwell’s army broke into the walled town on the Boyne and killed most of its garrison and many civilians, a massacre still remembered in Ireland.
A Highland charge led by Viscount Dundee routed government troops at the mouth of a Perthshire pass, but Dundee was killed in the moment of victory.
Fought in a snowstorm in Yorkshire, perhaps the bloodiest battle on English soil put Edward IV on the throne in the Wars of the Roses.
The first pitched battle of the English Civil War, below an escarpment in Warwickshire, ended without a winner.

event: Owain Glyndŵr is crowned Prince of Wales
note: The leader of the last great Welsh revolt against English rule held a parliament and was crowned at Machynlleth.
Caesar ringed the Gaulish hill fort in Burgundy with two lines of walls, beat off a relief army and forced Vercingetorix to surrender.
Spanish troops forced a whole French army to surrender in Andalusia, Napoleon’s first major defeat on land.
The people of the Aragonese city fought the French street by street and house by house for two months; some 50,000 died, most of them from disease, before it surrendered.
Hannibal trapped a Roman army in morning mist on the narrow shore of the Umbrian lake and destroyed it in three hours.

event: Constantine wins at the Milvian Bridge
note: After a vision of the cross, Constantine defeated his rival Maxentius at a bridge over the Tiber north of Rome and became master of the West.
Athens’ expedition to conquer Syracuse ended with its fleet destroyed in the harbour and its army captured; survivors were worked to death in the city’s quarries.
The Catholic Church’s answer to the Reformation met in the cathedral of the Alpine city of Trento, on and off, for eighteen years.

event: The Council of Constance ends the Great Schism
note: Meeting by Lake Constance, the council deposed rival popes, elected Martin V and had the Czech reformer Jan Hus burned at the stake.
The treaties signed in the Dutch city ended the War of the Spanish Succession; Britain gained Gibraltar and Newfoundland.
Lenin’s Russia made peace with Germany in the fortress of Brest-Litovsk, giving up Poland, the Baltic lands and Ukraine.
Germany, France and Belgium accepted their western borders at the Swiss lakeside town, and Germany was invited to join the League of Nations.
Senior Nazi officials met in a lakeside villa in a Berlin suburb to coordinate the murder of Europe’s Jews.

event: The Royal Observatory at Greenwich is founded
note: Charles II founded the observatory on a hill above the Thames to improve navigation; in 1884 its meridian became the zero of longitude.
The friar grew some 28,000 pea plants in the garden of St Thomas’s Abbey in Brno and worked out the laws of heredity.

event: The Augsburg Confession is read to the emperor
note: Lutheran princes presented their statement of faith to Charles V at the Diet in Augsburg; it is still the basic Lutheran creed.
Bishops meeting in the great church at Ephesus proclaimed Mary the Mother of God and condemned Nestorius, dividing the Church of the East from Rome.
Duke William of Aquitaine founded a Benedictine abbey in Burgundy free of local lords; it grew into the head of a network of over a thousand monasteries.

event: Columba founds the abbey on Iona
note: The Irish monk and his companions settled on a small island off Mull, from which they spread Christianity across Scotland.
The ruler of Kievan Rus’ accepted Christianity from Byzantium and had his people baptised in the Dnieper.
Bishops meeting across the Bosphorus from Constantinople defined Christ as one person in two natures, a decision that split off the Coptic and Armenian churches.
The East India Company beat the armies of the Mughal emperor and the nawabs of Bengal and Awadh on the Ganges, winning the right to tax Bengal.
The young Clive seized the fort at the Nawab of the Carnatic’s capital with 500 men and held it for 50 days, making his name.
Alexander beat a much larger Persian army on a narrow coastal plain at the north-eastern corner of the Mediterranean; Darius fled, leaving his family behind.
In his first victory over the Persians, Alexander led the cavalry charge across a river in north-western Anatolia and nearly lost his life.
Ottoman guns and muskets defeated Shah Ismail’s Safavid cavalry in north-western Iran, setting the Ottoman–Persian frontier for centuries.

event: Timur captures Sultan Bayezid at Ankara
note: Timur defeated the Ottomans north-east of Ankara and took the sultan prisoner; the Ottoman state nearly fell apart.
The Third Crusade’s two-year siege of the port ended when Saladin’s garrison surrendered to Richard I and Philip II of France.
Marching down the coast towards Jaffa, Richard the Lionheart’s army turned on Saladin’s harassing troops and beat them north of modern Tel Aviv.

event: The Manchus pass the Great Wall at Shanhai Pass
note: The Ming general Wu Sangui let the Manchus through the gate where the Great Wall meets the sea, and together they routed the rebel Li Zicheng; the Qing then took Beijing.
Soldiers rose against the Qing in the Yangtze city of Wuchang, now part of Wuhan; within months the last emperor had abdicated.
Chinese troops won their first major victory of the war with Japan in house-to-house fighting in a walled town on the Grand Canal.
During the Long March, Communist leaders meeting in a mansion in Guizhou gave Mao Zedong the leading role in the party.
Peasants, many of them Christians, held the ruined Hara Castle in Kyushu for three months; afterwards the shogunate closed Japan to most foreigners.
In a thunderstorm the young Oda Nobunaga surprised and killed the warlord Imagawa Yoshimoto in a narrow valley near modern Nagoya.
With only 13 ships, Yi Sun-sin used the fierce tidal currents of a narrow strait off south-west Korea to beat a Japanese fleet of over 130.
Korean soldiers, monks and civilians, women among them carrying stones in their aprons, held a hill fortress on the Han River against a Japanese army.
The first major battle between American and North Vietnamese troops was fought by helicopter-borne cavalry in the Central Highlands near the Cambodian border.
Indonesian fighters held out against British troops in the Javanese port for three weeks; the day it began is now Indonesia’s Heroes’ Day.
The island fortress at the mouth of Manila Bay held out under bombardment for five months before General Wainwright surrendered.
Twenty-one Sikh soldiers defended a signalling post on the North-West Frontier against thousands of Pashtun tribesmen until all were killed.
Charles Napier’s small army defeated the Talpur emirs of Sindh near Hyderabad; legend says he reported it with the one-word pun “Peccavi”.
Afghan forces under Ayub Khan routed a British-Indian brigade west of Kandahar; the heroine Malalai is said to have rallied the Afghan fighters.
A Persian army backed by Russia besieged the walled Afghan city for ten months; Britain’s alarm led to the First Anglo-Afghan War.
Russian troops under Skobelev breached the walls of the Turkmen fortress with a mine and massacred its defenders, completing Russia’s conquest of Central Asia.
A company of 108 Australians and New Zealanders held off a far larger Viet Cong force in a rubber plantation during a monsoon downpour.
Australian and Canadian battalions held a valley in central Korea against a Chinese offensive heading for Seoul.
The Mongol Yuan fleet destroyed the last Song fleet in the Pearl River delta; a minister leapt into the sea holding the boy emperor, ending the Song dynasty.
Jin armies captured the Song capital, then the richest city in the world, and carried off two emperors and thousands of courtiers to the north.
The Mongols besieged the twin Song fortress cities on the Han River for five years and finally broke them with counterweight catapults built by Persian engineers.
The Mughal emperor’s eight-month siege of the diamond-rich fortress near Hyderabad ended when a traitor opened a gate.
Akbar took the great Rajput fortress on its rock in Mewar after a four-month siege; its defenders died fighting and its women committed jauhar.
A Portuguese fleet destroyed the combined fleets of the Mamluks, Gujarat and Calicut off the island of Diu, winning Portugal control of the Indian Ocean.

event: Nalanda becomes a great Buddhist university
note: The monastery in Bihar taught monks from across Asia for some 700 years until it was sacked around 1200.

event: The Ananda Temple is completed at Bagan
note: King Kyansittha built one of the finest of the thousands of temples on the plain of Bagan by the Irrawaddy in Myanmar.

event: The temples of Prambanan are built
note: The largest Hindu temple complex in Indonesia, with towering shrines to Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma, rose in central Java soon after nearby Borobudur.
A British army marched 600 km into the Ethiopian highlands to free hostages; as they stormed his mountain fortress, Emperor Tewodros II shot himself.
Caesar defeated the Pompeian army and its Numidian allies on the coast of what is now Tunisia; Cato killed himself at Utica soon after.
A Moroccan army armed with muskets crossed the Sahara and defeated the Songhai Empire near Gao on the Niger.

event: Sundiata founds the Mali Empire at Kirina
note: Sundiata Keita defeated the sorcerer-king Sumanguru of Sosso, a victory still sung by griots in the Epic of Sundiata.
Rommel outflanked the British line in the Libyan desert, defeated the Eighth Army and went on to take Tobruk.
French troops stormed the city of bridges perched on a gorge in eastern Algeria at the second attempt.
French troops under Bugeaud defeated the Moroccan army near Oujda, ending Morocco’s support for the Algerian resistance leader Abd al-Qadir.
Boers dug in at the foot of the hills cut down the Highland Brigade at dawn as it advanced to relieve Kimberley.
Buller’s attempt to cross the Tugela River to relieve Ladysmith ended in defeat, completing Britain’s “Black Week”.
Royal Navy ships attacked the island town to depose its slave-trading king; ten years later Britain annexed it.
British warships and Free French forces under de Gaulle failed to persuade or force Vichy French West Africa’s capital to change sides.

event: British troops land at Diego Suarez
note: The Allies seized the great natural harbour at the northern tip of Vichy-held Madagascar to keep Japanese submarines out.
British and Indian troops fought for eight weeks up the mountain walls around the Eritrean town before the Italians gave way.
Emperor Haile Selassie’s last attack on the invading Italians failed in the northern highlands, and he went into exile five weeks later.
A British-Indian landing at the East African port was beaten off by Lettow-Vorbeck’s much smaller force, helped by swarms of angry bees.
The great theologian died as the Vandals besieged his city on the coast of what is now Algeria.
The emperor’s fleet took the fortress of La Goulette and Tunis from the corsair Barbarossa and freed thousands of Christian captives.
One of the bloodiest battles of the War of 1812 was fought at night within earshot of Niagara Falls; both sides claimed victory.
British ships shelled the fort guarding Baltimore harbour all night; seeing its flag still flying at dawn, Francis Scott Key wrote “The Star-Spangled Banner”.
British troops set fire to the Capitol, the White House and other public buildings, in revenge for the American burning of York in Canada.
General Anthony Wayne’s army defeated a Native confederacy among storm-felled trees by the Maumee River, near modern Toledo, Ohio.
Daniel Morgan’s Patriots trapped Banastre Tarleton’s British force with a feigned retreat in a South Carolina pasture.
Union troops made wave after wave of hopeless attacks on Confederates behind a stone wall on Marye’s Heights above the town.
Lee split his army and routed a much larger Union army in the Virginia woods, but Stonewall Jackson was shot by his own men.
The Confederates’ greatest victory in the West, in the woods of north-west Georgia, left the Union army besieged at Chattanooga.

event: The First Battle of Bull Run
note: Picnickers from Washington watched the first big battle of the Civil War at Manassas, Virginia, where Thomas Jackson earned the name “Stonewall”.
On Santa Anna’s orders, Mexican troops shot over 340 Texan prisoners outside the presidio of La Bahía; “Remember Goliad!” became a battle cry.
Álvaro Obregón’s trenches and machine guns broke Pancho Villa’s cavalry charges in the Bajío, the turning point of the Mexican Revolution.
Pancho Villa’s Division of the North stormed the hills around the silver-mining city in the bloodiest battle of the revolution.
Zachary Taylor’s American army took the northern Mexican city street by street, early in the Mexican–American War.
Delegates from 44 nations met at a grand hotel in the White Mountains of New Hampshire and created the IMF and the World Bank.

event: The United Nations Charter is signed
note: Delegates from 50 countries signed the charter in San Francisco’s Veterans War Memorial Building after two months of talks.
After thirteen days at the presidential retreat in the Maryland hills, Sadat and Begin agreed a framework for peace between Egypt and Israel.
Theodore Roosevelt brokered the end of the Russo-Japanese War at the navy yard near Portsmouth, New Hampshire, and won the Nobel Peace Prize.
The French explorer sailed up the St Lawrence to an Iroquoian town below a mountain he named Mont Royal, where Montreal now stands.

event: La Salle claims Louisiana for France
note: After canoeing down the Mississippi, La Salle reached its mouth and claimed the whole basin for Louis XIV.
After a winter trapped in the ice of James Bay, his mutinous crew set Hudson, his son and seven men adrift in a small boat; they were never seen again.

event: Pueblo Bonito rises in Chaco Canyon
note: Ancestral Puebloans built a D-shaped great house of some 650 rooms in a New Mexico canyon, the hub of a network of roads.
The Zapotecs levelled a mountaintop above the Oaxaca valley to build one of the first cities in Mesoamerica.

event: The Gate of the Sun is carved at Tiwanaku
note: The Tiwanaku culture carved the monolithic gateway near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca in Bolivia.
Bolívar’s cavalry beat the royalists with lances and swords, without a shot fired, on a high Andean plain in Peru.
Manuel Belgrano disobeyed orders to retreat and beat a royalist army at the northern Argentine city, saving the revolution.
Justo José de Urquiza’s army defeated the dictator Juan Manuel de Rosas outside Buenos Aires, and Rosas fled into exile in England.
Portuguese-Brazilian, Indigenous and African fighters defeated the Dutch on hills south of Recife, beginning the end of Dutch Brazil.

event: The charge up San Juan Hill
note: American troops, including Theodore Roosevelt’s Rough Riders, took the heights above Santiago de Cuba from the Spanish.
Guevara’s rebels derailed an armoured train and captured the central Cuban city; Batista fled the country the next day.
A British squadron captured the Spanish treasure port on Panama’s Caribbean coast with six ships; London’s Portobello Road is named after the victory.
Costa Rican troops defeated the American filibuster William Walker in a Nicaraguan town; the drummer boy Juan Santamaría died setting fire to the inn the invaders held.
The Chilean army broke Peru’s defences south of Lima in the War of the Pacific and occupied the capital days later.
Chilean ironclads cornered and captured the Peruvian Huáscar off the coast of the Atacama; Admiral Grau died on her bridge.
The Brazilian navy destroyed Paraguay’s river fleet on the Paraná near Corrientes, cutting Paraguay off from the sea.
A Spanish fleet shelled the undefended Chilean port for three hours, destroying its warehouses, in a war over Spain’s ambitions in the Pacific.
Peruvian shore batteries fought the same Spanish fleet to a standstill outside Peru’s main port, and the Spanish sailed home.

event: The Battle of the Coral Sea
note: The first naval battle fought entirely by aircraft, with the fleets never in sight of each other, stopped a Japanese invasion of Port Moresby.
Australian and American troops took the Japanese beachheads on the north coast of Papua in swampy jungle at a terrible cost.
US Marines on the tiny Pacific atoll beat off one Japanese landing before a second overwhelmed them.
A Japanese cruiser force sank four Allied cruisers in a night action off Guadalcanal, one of the worst defeats in the history of the US Navy.
Māori defenders of a fortified pā near Tauranga repulsed a British assault after a heavy bombardment, and gave water to the enemy wounded.
British troops took the elaborate pā of the Māori leader Kawiti in Northland, ending the Flagstaff War.
Japanese troops overwhelmed the small Australian garrison and turned the harbour on New Britain into their great base in the South Pacific.
American carrier aircraft sank dozens of ships at Japan’s fleet anchorage in the Caroline Islands; the wrecks now draw divers from around the world.
The Abbasid victory over a Tang Chinese army by the Talas River marked the western limit of Chinese power in Central Asia. The exact field is unknown, but it lay near modern Taraz and Talas.

Robert Clive’s East India Company army defeated the Nawab of Bengal at Palashi on the Bhagirathi, north of Calcutta, after bribing the Nawab’s commander, Mir Jafar: the start of British rule in India.

event: Babur defeats the Sultan of Delhi
note: Babur’s smaller army, using field guns and flanking cavalry, killed Sultan Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat, north of Delhi, and founded the Mughal Empire.
The largest land battle of the Persian Wars was fought below the town of Plataea in Boeotia; the Spartan-led Greek army killed Mardonius and ended the Persian invasion of Greece.
Alexander broke Darius III’s huge army on a plain in northern Mesopotamia, probably near Tel Gomel north-east of Mosul, opening Babylon and Persia to the Macedonians.
Germanic tribes under Arminius ambushed Varus’s army in the Teutoburg Forest; finds since 1987 place the main fighting at Kalkriese, north of Osnabrück.
Scipio Africanus defeated Hannibal in what is now northern Tunisia, ending the Second Punic War; the battlefield, somewhere near Zama Regia, has never been located.

event: Saladin destroys the crusader army at Hattin
note: Saladin trapped the thirsty crusader army on the twin peaks of an extinct volcano west of the Sea of Galilee; three months later he took Jerusalem.

event: The Mamluks halt the Mongols at Ain Jalut
note: The Mamluks of Egypt under Qutuz and Baybars defeated a Mongol army at the spring of Goliath in the Jezreel Valley, stopping the Mongol advance into the Levant and Africa.
The Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan defeated and captured the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV north of Lake Van, opening Anatolia to Turkish settlement.

event: Japan annihilates the Russian fleet at Tsushima
note: Admiral Togo’s fleet destroyed the Russian Baltic Fleet, which had sailed halfway round the world, in the strait between Korea and Japan; Russia soon sued for peace.
About 150 British soldiers, many sick or wounded, held a mission station on the Buffalo River against some 4,000 Zulus; eleven of the defenders won the Victoria Cross.
Emperor Menelik II’s army routed an Italian invasion force in the mountains of Tigray, preserving Ethiopia’s independence through the age of European empire in Africa.
Fletcher Christian’s mutineers set Captain Bligh and 18 loyal men adrift near Tofua in Tonga; Bligh sailed the open launch 6,700 km to Timor, while the mutineers hid on Pitcairn Island.
Sam Houston’s Texians surprised Santa Anna’s army during its afternoon rest beside the San Jacinto River, east of modern Houston, winning Texas its independence in 18 minutes.
Antonio José de Sucre’s army defeated the last great royalist army on the plain of Quinua in the Peruvian Andes, sealing South America’s independence from Spain.
Simón Bolívar’s army, fresh from crossing the Andes, defeated the Spanish at a bridge south of Tunja; three days later he entered Bogotá.

event: Pizarro captures the Inca emperor Atahualpa
note: Francisco Pizarro’s 168 Spaniards ambushed Atahualpa’s retinue in the main square of the Andean town of Cajamarca and took the emperor hostage.

event: Mao’s Long March comes to an end
note: After a fighting retreat of about 10,000 km from Jiangxi, Mao’s First Front Army reached the communist base at Wuqi in northern Shaanxi with perhaps a tenth of the men who set out.

event: The first atomic bomb is tested
note: The world’s first nuclear explosion, a plutonium device, lit up the Jornada del Muerto desert in New Mexico before dawn, about 55 km south-east of Socorro.
Donald Johanson and Tom Gray found the 3.2-million-year-old skeleton of an Australopithecus afarensis at Hadar in Ethiopia’s Afar region; she was named after a Beatles song.

event: An Anglo-Saxon ship burial is unearthed
note: Excavators uncovered the imprint of a 27 m ship, packed with treasures including a famous helmet, in a burial mound at Sutton Hoo near Woodbridge in Suffolk; it is probably the grave of King Rædwald.
Monks Mound, the largest earthwork in pre-Columbian America, stood at the heart of the Mississippian city of Cahokia, across the Mississippi from modern St Louis.

event: ‘Bloody Sunday’ on the march from Selma
note: State troopers beat civil rights marchers, among them John Lewis, at the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama; the outcry helped pass the Voting Rights Act.

event: Harold II defeats the Norwegian invasion
note: Harold Godwinson surprised and killed Harald Hardrada of Norway at Stamford Bridge, east of York; three days later William landed in Sussex, and Harold had to march south to Hastings.

event: Richard III is killed at Bosworth Field
note: Henry Tudor’s victory, in which Richard III became the last English king to die in battle, ended the Wars of the Roses; finds since 2009 place the fighting about 3 km south-west of the traditional site.
Marlborough and Prince Eugene destroyed a Franco-Bavarian army beside the Danube at Blindheim (Blenheim) in Bavaria, saving Vienna; Blenheim Palace was the nation’s reward to Marlborough.

event: Peter the Great defeats Sweden at Poltava
note: Peter the Great’s army destroyed Charles XII’s Swedish army outside the Ukrainian town of Poltava, ending Sweden’s time as a great power.
British and Indian troops held a ridge in the Naga Hills, at one point fighting across the district commissioner’s tennis court, and helped halt the Japanese invasion of India.
The world’s first artificial satellite was launched from Tyuratam (later Baikonur) on the steppe of Soviet Kazakhstan; its radio beeps could be picked up around the world.
An asteroid or comet fragment exploded in the air over the Siberian taiga near the Podkamennaya Tunguska River, flattening some 80 million trees over 2,150 km².
The largest eruption in recorded history, on the island of Sumbawa in Indonesia, killed tens of thousands and caused the ‘Year Without a Summer’ across the northern hemisphere in 1816.
Mary Leakey found the skull of Paranthropus boisei in Olduvai Gorge, on the edge of the Serengeti in Tanzania, putting East Africa at the centre of the search for human origins.

event: The stone circles of Göbekli Tepe are raised
note: Hunter-gatherers raised rings of carved, T-shaped limestone pillars on a hilltop near Şanlıurfa in south-east Turkey, some 6,000 years before Stonehenge.

event: The last stand of the samurai
note: Saigō Takamori and his last few hundred samurai were overwhelmed by the new conscript army on Shiroyama hill above Kagoshima, ending the Satsuma Rebellion.

event: The Peace of Westphalia ends the Thirty Years’ War
note: The treaties were negotiated in the Westphalian towns of Münster and Osnabrück and signed in Münster, whose town hall still has its Hall of Peace.

event: Martin Luther refuses to recant before the emperor
note: At the imperial diet in Worms on the Rhine, Luther refused to disown his writings before Charles V; declared an outlaw, he was spirited away to the Wartburg castle.

event: Andrew Jackson repels a British assault
note: Jackson’s mix of regulars, militia, free Black volunteers and pirates beat off a British attack at Chalmette, just below New Orleans, unaware that peace had been signed two weeks earlier.
US 7th Cavalry troops killed some 250 Lakota men, women and children while disarming Spotted Elk’s band beside Wounded Knee Creek on the Pine Ridge Reservation, South Dakota.
Antonio José de Sucre’s army defeated the Spanish on the slopes of the Pichincha volcano above Quito, freeing what is now Ecuador.

event: The Cathars’ last mountain stronghold falls
note: After a ten-month siege of the castle on its crag in the Pyrenean foothills, more than 200 Cathars who would not recant were burned at its foot.

event: “Kill them all; God will know his own”
note: Crusaders against the Cathar heresy stormed a city in Languedoc and slaughtered its people, Catholics and heretics alike.

event: Henry IV grants toleration to the Huguenots
note: The edict signed in the Breton city on the Loire ended France’s Wars of Religion by giving Protestants freedom of worship in many places.

event: Richelieu starves out the Huguenot stronghold
note: The cardinal sealed the Atlantic port off with a stone dyke across its harbour; some 20,000 of its 27,000 people died before it surrendered.

event: A young artillery officer named Bonaparte makes his name
note: Napoleon’s guns drove the British and Spanish fleets out of the great Mediterranean naval base that French royalists had handed to them.

event: Napoleon’s narrow victory over the Austrians
note: Losing by mid-afternoon on the plain of Piedmont, Napoleon was saved by the arrival of General Desaix, who was killed leading the counter-attack.

event: A battle fought in a snowstorm
note: Napoleon and the Russians fought to a bloody draw in a blizzard in East Prussia, in what is now the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad.

event: Napoleon’s first defeat in a decade
note: Archduke Charles threw the French back across the Danube near Vienna after the flooded river broke their pontoon bridge.

event: Wellington captures King Joseph’s baggage train
note: The rout of the French army in the Basque Country ended Napoleon’s rule in Spain; British soldiers stopped to loot a fortune in coin.

event: Nelson boards two enemy ships in a row
note: Commodore Nelson broke out of line and captured one Spanish ship by boarding it from another, off the south-west tip of Portugal.
Using a ridge to hide his march, Frederick fell on the flank of an Austrian army twice the size of his own in Silesia, west of Breslau.

event: “Gentlemen of the French Guard, fire first!”
note: Marshal de Saxe’s French army beat the British, Dutch and Hanoverians south-east of Tournai in what is now Belgium.

event: The last British king to lead his troops in battle
note: George II led his army on foot to beat the French by the River Main east of Frankfurt; Handel wrote a Te Deum for the victory.

event: The teenage Charles XII routs the Russians in a blizzard
note: The 18-year-old Swedish king attacked a Russian army four times the size of his own that was besieging a fortress on the Estonian border.
The Russian general took the Ottoman stronghold near the mouth of the Danube by storm in a single day; the slaughter was immense.

event: The raid to block a U-boat base
note: British ships tried to sink blockships in the canal mouth of a Belgian port used by German submarines; eight Victoria Crosses were won.

event: “The black day of the German army”
note: Allied tanks and infantry broke through east of a French cathedral city, beginning the Hundred Days Offensive that ended the war.

event: The battles for an iron-ore port
note: British, French, Polish and Norwegian forces fought the Germans for a harbour in northern Norway that shipped Swedish iron ore.
German paratroopers seized the airfield at Maleme and took the Greek island from British and Commonwealth forces, but lost so many men that Hitler never tried it again.

event: Americans capture a Rhine bridge intact
note: German demolition charges failed to bring down the railway bridge south of Bonn, and American troops raced across it.
Patrols of the two armies advancing from east and west met on the Elbe at Torgau in Saxony, cutting Germany in two.
Mark Antony and Octavian beat Caesar’s assassins in two battles in eastern Macedonia, and both Brutus and Cassius took their own lives.

event: Gladiators break out of their school
note: Spartacus and about 70 gladiators escaped from a training school at Capua, near Naples, and raised an army of slaves that beat several Roman armies.

event: Boudica burns the first Roman capital of Britain
note: The queen of the Iceni sacked Camulodunum, now Colchester, then London and St Albans, before the Romans crushed her army.

event: An emperor retires to grow cabbages
note: Diocletian gave up the throne and lived in his vast seaside palace on the Dalmatian coast; the old town of Split grew up inside its walls.

event: Vikings defeat the men of Essex
note: Ealdorman Byrhtnoth let the Vikings cross a causeway from their island camp to fight on fair ground, and was killed; an Old English poem tells the story.
Seven countries took part at a theatre in the Swiss lakeside town of Lugano, and the host country’s Lys Assia won.

event: Wagner opens his own festival theatre
note: The composer built a theatre with a hidden orchestra pit in a small Franconian town just to stage The Ring; the festival still plays only his works.
Twelve European countries set up a physics laboratory on the Swiss–French border near Geneva; the World Wide Web was invented there in 1989.

event: Copernicus puts the Sun at the centre
note: The canon of a cathedral by the Vistula Lagoon in Poland is said to have seen the first printed copy of his book on the day he died.
Alessandro Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by brine-soaked cloth and produced a steady current; he lived in Como, on its lake in Lombardy.
Karl Benz patented his three-wheeled car in Mannheim; his wife Bertha took it on the first long-distance drive two years later.
Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin’s first rigid airship rose from a floating hangar on Lake Constance and flew for 18 minutes.
The octagonal chapel at the heart of Charlemagne’s favourite residence became the church where German kings were crowned for 600 years.
The great army of Danes took the Northumbrian city and made it Jorvik, capital of a Viking kingdom.

event: The Scots tell the pope they will never submit
note: Barons and freeholders wrote to Pope John XXII that they fought “for freedom alone”; the letter was probably drafted at an abbey on the Angus coast.
The Gaelic lords of Ulster sailed into exile from Lough Swilly in Donegal, opening their lands to the Plantation of Ulster.

event: The Chartists march on a Welsh town
note: Several thousand Chartists demanding the vote marched on the Westgate Hotel in Newport, Monmouthshire, where soldiers opened fire and killed over twenty.

event: A Catalan city falls to the Bourbons
note: Philip V’s army stormed the city after a 14-month siege, ending Catalonia’s separate institutions; the date is now Catalonia’s national day.

event: The first battle of ironclad fleets
note: The Austrian navy beat a larger Italian fleet off an Adriatic island by ramming, which led navies to fit rams to warships for decades.

event: A Ming emperor is captured by the Mongols
note: The Zhengtong Emperor led a huge army out beyond the Great Wall and was taken prisoner by Esen Taishi’s Oirats at a fort north-west of Beijing.

event: Britain’s first embassy to the Qianlong Emperor
note: Lord Macartney was received at the summer retreat of Chengde beyond the Great Wall; the emperor replied that China had no need of Britain’s goods.

event: The forty-seven rōnin avenge their master
note: Masterless samurai stormed Kira Yoshinaka’s mansion in Edo and carried his head to their lord’s grave; they were then ordered to commit seppuku.

event: The Japanese invasion of Korea begins
note: Hideyoshi’s army landed at the southern port and took its fortress in a day, beginning seven years of war.

event: Admiral Yi dies in his last battle
note: Yi Sun-sin was shot as his fleet destroyed the Japanese ships leaving Korea; he told his men to hide his death until the battle was won.

event: The Dutch East India Company builds its capital
note: Jan Pieterszoon Coen razed the town of Jayakarta on Java and built Batavia on its ruins; it is now Jakarta.

event: The Dutch conquer the nutmeg islands
note: Coen’s men killed or enslaved most of the people of the Banda Islands in the Moluccas, then the only source of nutmeg in the world.

event: A Javanese prince is seized at peace talks
note: The Dutch arrested Prince Diponegoro at Magelang, ending a five-year war that cost some 200,000 lives.
Commodore Dewey’s American squadron destroyed the Spanish fleet off Cavite in a morning without losing a man in action.
Spain executed the novelist and reformer by firing squad in the park by Manila Bay now named after him; his death fired the Philippine Revolution.
The Deccan sultanates crushed the great Hindu empire of the south, and its capital at Hampi was looted for months.

event: Shivaji kills Afzal Khan with tiger claws
note: Meeting the Bijapur general below his hill fort in the Western Ghats, the Maratha leader killed him with steel claws hidden in his hand.
A small East India Company force, mostly Mahar soldiers, held a village on the Bhima river against the Peshwa’s army; Dalits still gather at its obelisk.

event: The warrior queen of 1857 dies in battle
note: Lakshmibai, the Rani of Jhansi, who led rebels in the Indian Rebellion, was killed fighting British cavalry near the fortress of Gwalior.
Gandhi took up the cause of tenant farmers forced to grow indigo for British planters in a district of northern Bihar, and won.
Chiefs of the hill kingdom signed it over to the British in the royal audience hall at Kandy, beside the Temple of the Tooth.
The Persian ruler crushed the Mughal army north of Delhi in three hours, then sacked the capital and carried off the Peacock Throne.

event: A British army surrenders after a 147-day siege
note: Starving British and Indian troops in a loop of the Tigris surrendered to the Ottomans; most of the prisoners died on the march that followed.

event: Crusaders take a great Syrian city
note: After an eight-month siege a traitor let the First Crusade over the walls of Antioch; the crusaders were then besieged in turn and saved, they believed, by the Holy Lance.

event: Alexander builds a causeway to an island city
note: Alexander’s engineers built a mole out to the Phoenician island city of Tyre and took it after seven months; the causeway turned the island into a peninsula.
An Egyptian army sent by the Ottomans destroyed the mud-brick capital of the first Saudi state; its ruins lie on the edge of modern Riyadh.

event: A young exile seizes a mud-brick fort at dawn
note: Ibn Saud and about forty men took the Masmak fort in Riyadh, the first step towards founding the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

event: The great dam of Saba bursts
note: The final collapse of the ancient dam at Ma’rib in Yemen, built over a thousand years earlier, is remembered in the Quran and scattered the region’s tribes.

event: The Mongols annihilate a great oasis city
note: Tolui’s army slaughtered the people of Merv, one of the largest cities in the world, in what is now Turkmenistan; it never recovered.

event: Cossacks take the Siberian khanate’s capital
note: Yermak’s Cossacks defeated Khan Kuchum and took Qashliq on the Irtysh, near modern Tobolsk, opening Siberia to Russia.

event: A French king is captured in Egypt
note: The Mamluks trapped the crusaders in the streets of Mansurah in the Nile delta; Louis IX was captured soon after, and the Mamluks then seized power in Egypt.

event: The shogun’s army is routed outside the old capital
note: Troops loyal to the emperor, with modern rifles, beat a larger shogunate army south of Kyoto, the opening battle of the Boshin War.

event: The short-lived Republic of Ezo falls
note: The last shogunate loyalists, with French advisers, held a star-shaped fort on Hokkaido until the new imperial navy and army forced their surrender.

event: A bloody draw with the Sikhs
note: The East India Company’s army lost some 2,400 men attacking through thick jungle near the Jhelum in Punjab; Britain annexed the Punjab weeks later.

event: The last Burmese kings build a new royal city
note: King Mindon laid out a square walled city with a moat and a teak palace at its heart; the British exiled the last king from it in 1885.

event: Japan’s first landing of the Pacific war
note: Japanese troops came ashore on the north-east coast of Malaya about an hour before the attack on Pearl Harbor.

event: An English adventurer becomes a rajah
note: The Sultan of Brunei made James Brooke Rajah of Sarawak in northern Borneo, founding a dynasty of “White Rajahs” that ruled from Kuching for a century.

event: A small army routs a huge one on a riverbank
note: The Eastern Jin defeated the much larger Former Qin army in Anhui; panic spread as the fleeing soldiers heard the enemy in every gust of wind.
Cao Cao burned his rival’s grain stores and won a battle near the Yellow River that gave him northern China.

event: Emperor Quang Trung routs a Qing army
note: The Tây Sơn ruler marched his army north for the lunar new year and drove the Chinese occupiers out of Thăng Long, now Hanoi.

event: The British advance on Baghdad is stopped
note: Ottoman troops halted a British-Indian army beside the great brick arch of the ancient Persian capital, and the British fell back to Kut.

event: The First Crusade wins its first battle
note: The crusaders beat the Seljuk sultan Kilij Arslan in Anatolia, near modern Eskişehir, opening the road across Asia Minor.
King David the Builder beat a much larger Seljuk army in the hills west of Tbilisi and took back the city the next year.

event: Great Buddhas are carved into a granite cliff
note: King Parakramabahu I had four Buddha images carved from one rock face at Polonnaruwa in Sri Lanka, among them a 14 m reclining Buddha.

event: Japan takes a German colony in China
note: Japanese and British forces besieged the German naval base on the Shandong coast, a town best known today for its German-founded brewery.

event: A British square is broken in the desert
note: Mahdist warriors broke into a square of the camel corps marching to relieve Khartoum, but were driven off with heavy losses.

event: Free French troops hold a desert fort
note: General Koenig’s Free French brigade held an old Ottoman fort in the Libyan desert against Rommel for two weeks; a Paris bridge is named after it.
A French army landed on a beach west of Algiers and took the city three weeks later, beginning 132 years of French rule.

event: The French take the Merina capital
note: A French expedition shelled the royal palace on the hilltop of Madagascar’s capital until Queen Ranavalona III surrendered.

event: The “Lunatic Express” reaches a swampy depot
note: The railway from Mombasa set up a depot by a cold stream on the plains, and it grew into Nairobi, Kenya’s capital.

event: Young Christian converts are burned alive
note: King Mwanga of Buganda had pages at his court burned at Namugongo, near Kampala; Pope Paul VI declared them saints in 1964.
British aircraft bombed the stone forts of Taleh, ending the 20-year resistance of the Dervish leader Mohammed Abdullah Hassan, whom the British called the Mad Mullah.

event: A pharaoh builds a new capital for his one god
note: Akhenaten founded Akhetaten on empty desert land by the Nile to worship the sun disc, the Aten; it was abandoned soon after his death.

event: A woman pharaoh builds her terraced temple
note: Hatshepsut’s colonnaded temple rises in three terraces against the cliffs at Deir el-Bahari, across the Nile from Luxor.
King Piye marched north from his capital at Napata, below a sacred flat-topped mountain in Sudan, and made himself pharaoh.

event: Voortrekkers hold off an army from a wagon laager
note: About 40 Boer men in a circle of wagons in the Free State beat off thousands of Mzilikazi’s Ndebele warriors, who drove off their cattle.

event: The Funj found a sultanate on the Blue Nile
note: Amara Dunqas founded a kingdom with its capital at Sennar that ruled much of Sudan for three centuries.

event: Bronzes are cast in the Niger forest
note: Smiths in what is now south-east Nigeria cast intricate bronze vessels and regalia, found by a man digging a cistern in 1938.

event: An empress chooses a site for a new capital
note: Empress Taytu picked a place by hot springs in the Ethiopian highlands, and Menelik II made it his capital, “New Flower”.
The founder of the Basotho nation moved his people to a flat-topped mountain near modern Maseru that no attacker ever took.

event: An Egyptian army under a British officer is annihilated
note: The Mahdi’s forces destroyed Hicks Pasha’s column of 10,000 men in the forest of Kordofan, making the Mahdi master of most of Sudan.
Cambyses II beat Psamtik III at the eastern gateway of the Nile delta; Herodotus said the Persians used cats, sacred to the Egyptians, as shields.

event: The “Lion of the Desert” is hanged
note: Italy hanged the 73-year-old Libyan resistance leader in front of 20,000 prisoners at Suluq in Cyrenaica.

event: An Ottoman fleet routs a Christian armada
note: Piyale Pasha’s fleet destroyed a Spanish-led fleet off an island in the Gulf of Gabès, the high point of Ottoman sea power in the Mediterranean.

event: A young lawyer sets out on a 29-year journey
note: At 21, Ibn Battuta left his home town of Tangier on pilgrimage to Mecca and kept travelling, to China, India and Mali, before he came home.

event: Eighty soldiers are lured into an ambush
note: Crazy Horse’s decoys drew Captain Fetterman’s command over a ridge near Fort Phil Kearny in Wyoming, where Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors killed them all.

event: Union miners blow a crater under Confederate lines
note: Pennsylvania coal miners dug a tunnel under the defences of Petersburg, Virginia, and blew them up, but the attack that followed was a disaster.
A wagon train bound for California was trapped by snow in the Sierra Nevada beside a lake now named after it; only about half survived.

event: The Pueblo Revolt drives out the Spanish
note: Pueblo peoples led by Popé rose together and besieged the Spanish colonial capital of New Mexico until the settlers fled south.
When the governor returned with supplies after three years, the English settlers on an island off North Carolina had vanished, leaving only the word “CROATOAN” carved on a post.
Colonial militia attacked a fortified Narragansett village in a frozen swamp in Rhode Island, killing hundreds, during King Philip’s War.

event: The Green Mountain Boys seize a fort
note: Ethan Allen and Benedict Arnold took the British fort on Lake Champlain at dawn without a shot; its cannon were later dragged to Boston.
American troops defeated the British and their Native allies on the Thames River in Upper Canada; the Shawnee leader Tecumseh was killed.
The Métis seized Upper Fort Garry, now in Winnipeg, and set up their own government; the province of Manitoba was created on their terms.

event: A mountainside buries a mining town
note: About 110 million tonnes of limestone fell from Turtle Mountain in Alberta in 100 seconds, burying part of the town of Frank.

event: Amundsen winters on the Northwest Passage
note: Amundsen’s small sloop spent two winters in a sheltered harbour on King William Island, where he learned polar survival from the Netsilik Inuit.

event: The first great American silver strike
note: Miners in Nevada found a rich vein of silver, and Virginia City boomed into one of the richest towns in the West.

event: A Habsburg emperor is shot in Mexico
note: The Austrian archduke whom Napoleon III had made emperor of Mexico was executed with two generals on the Hill of Bells outside Querétaro.

event: Brigham Young’s pioneers reach their promised valley
note: “This is the right place,” Young is said to have declared, and the Latter-day Saints began building Salt Lake City.

event: A dispute over a golf course becomes an armed standoff
note: Mohawks blocked a road near Montreal to stop a golf course being built on a burial ground; the army was called in for 78 days.

event: The largest armed uprising since the Civil War
note: About 10,000 striking coal miners marched to unionise southern West Virginia and fought deputies and troops on a ridge for five days.
The planter Carlos Manuel de Céspedes freed his slaves at his sugar mill, La Demajagua, near Manzanillo, and called for independence from Spain.

event: A Mapuche leader defeats the conquistador who owned him
note: Lautaro, once Pedro de Valdivia’s groom, destroyed his small force at a fort in southern Chile; Valdivia was captured and killed.

event: The largest battle in South American history
note: Paraguay’s army attacked the Brazilian, Argentine and Uruguayan allies in the swamps of southern Paraguay and was cut to pieces.

event: The army destroys a backlands holy city
note: The Brazilian army needed four expeditions to destroy a community of 25,000 followers of the preacher Antônio Conselheiro in Bahia.

event: The fall of a kingdom of escaped slaves
note: Palmares, in the hills of north-east Brazil, held out against the Portuguese and Dutch for almost a century; its last leader, Zumbi, was killed in 1695.

event: Maya murals of battle and celebration
note: Artists painted three rooms of a temple in the Chiapas rainforest with battles, prisoners and a royal festival; outsiders first saw them in 1946.

event: A European first sees the Pacific from the Americas
note: The Spanish conquistador Balboa climbed a peak in the Darién isthmus and saw the ocean he called the South Sea.
Admiral Rodney broke the French line between Guadeloupe and Dominica and captured Admiral de Grasse, saving Jamaica for Britain.
The Santa María ran aground off the north coast of Hispaniola, in present-day Haiti; Columbus built a fort from her timbers and left 39 men, none of whom survived.

event: The largest adobe city in the Americas
note: The Chimú capital on the desert coast of northern Peru covered 20 km² with mud-brick palaces before the Inca conquered it around 1470.

event: One of the oldest cities in the Americas
note: People in a desert valley north of Lima built pyramids and sunken plazas while the Great Pyramid was rising in Egypt.

event: The Toltecs raise their stone warriors
note: Giant columns carved as warriors stand on a pyramid at the Toltec capital north of Mexico City.

event: The conquistadors survive a desperate battle
note: Fleeing Tenochtitlan after the Noche Triste, Cortés’s battered force broke an Aztec army north-east of the valley of Mexico by killing its commander.
Bernardo O’Higgins’ troops were besieged in a town south of Santiago and broke out; Spain then held Chile for three more years.

event: A plot against Portuguese rule in Brazil’s gold country
note: Conspirators in Vila Rica, now Ouro Preto, planned a republic; the dentist Tiradentes was hanged for it and is now a national hero.

event: Cuba’s poet of independence dies in his first battle
note: José Martí rode into a Spanish column at Dos Ríos in eastern Cuba weeks after landing, and was shot.
Paul Bogle led a protest march on the courthouse of a Jamaican town; Governor Eyre’s brutal repression caused a scandal in Britain.
American and German warships facing off over Samoa stayed in Apia harbour as a hurricane struck; only one British ship steamed out and survived.
King Cakobau and the chiefs signed the Deed of Cession at Levuka, the old capital on the island of Ovalau.

event: Troops march into a peaceful Māori village
note: The village of the prophets Te Whiti and Tohu, who preached passive resistance to land confiscation, met the soldiers with children singing.

event: The Pink and White Terraces are destroyed
note: A volcanic eruption in New Zealand’s North Island buried villages and destroyed the silica terraces, then a famous tourist sight.

event: A convict prison opens on a guarded peninsula
note: Re-offending convicts were sent to the settlement on Tasmania’s Tasman Peninsula, cut off by a narrow neck guarded by a line of chained dogs.

event: A future president’s patrol boat is cut in two
note: A Japanese destroyer rammed John F. Kennedy’s boat in the Solomon Islands; he swam his crew to a small island, where scouts found them days later.

event: Shackleton’s men wait on a rocky island
note: Twenty-two men lived under two upturned boats on Elephant Island for four months while Shackleton sailed 1,300 km to South Georgia for help; all survived.
The Commonwealth of Australia was proclaimed before a crowd of 60,000 in Centennial Park, Sydney.
Some 300 Māori men and women held a hastily built pā in the Waikato against British troops for three days and refused to surrender.

event: Islanders build a city of basalt on a reef
note: The Saudeleur dynasty built nearly 100 artificial islets of stacked basalt columns off Pohnpei in Micronesia.

event: Spain and Portugal sign the Treaty of Tordesillas
note: The two crowns split newly charted lands along a meridian 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands. The treaty was signed in this Castilian town on the Douro, near Valladolid.
Sun Quan and Liu Bei’s allied fleet used fire ships to rout Cao Cao on the Yangtze, ensuring China split into three kingdoms; the most widely accepted site is the cliffs at Chibi in Hubei.

event: Admiral Yi’s victory at Hansan Island
note: Yi Sun-sin lured a Japanese fleet out of a narrow strait and destroyed it off Hansan Island in a ‘crane wing’ formation, cutting Japan’s sea supply line during its invasion of Korea.
Julius Caesar beat Pompey’s larger army on the plain beside the Enipeus river near Pharsalus in Thessaly; Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was murdered.

event: Parthian horse archers destroy Crassus’s legions
note: Parthian cavalry shot Marcus Licinius Crassus’s army to pieces on the open plain near Carrhae (Harran) in what is now south-east Turkey; Crassus was killed during truce talks.

event: The Goths kill Emperor Valens in battle
note: Gothic warriors destroyed the eastern Roman field army outside Adrianople (Edirne) in Thrace and killed the emperor Valens: a turning point in Rome’s struggle with the barbarians.

event: Aetius checks Attila on the Catalaunian Plains
note: A Roman and Visigothic army under Flavius Aetius halted Attila’s Huns in Champagne. The exact battlefield is unknown, somewhere between Troyes and Châlons-en-Champagne.
Arab Muslim armies under Khalid ibn al-Walid routed the Byzantines by the Yarmouk river, south-east of the Sea of Galilee, ending Byzantine rule in Syria.

event: Otto the Great defeats the Magyars
note: Otto I’s German army crushed the Hungarian raiders on the Lech floodplain near Augsburg, ending decades of Magyar raids into western Europe.

event: Suleiman the Magnificent crushes Hungary at Mohács
note: The Ottoman army destroyed the Hungarian army on the Danube plain south of Mohács; King Louis II drowned in flight, and Hungary was carved up for 150 years.

event: Voortrekkers defeat the Zulu army at Blood River
note: About 470 Voortrekkers in a laager of 64 wagons beside the Ncome River repulsed a Zulu army of some 15,000; three Boers were wounded and about 3,000 Zulus killed.
Cuban and Angolan troops held the town against South African and UNITA forces in Africa’s largest battle since the Second World War; the stalemate led to Namibian independence.

event: British forces capture the fortress of Louisbourg
note: Amherst and Wolfe took France’s great fortress on Cape Breton Island after a seven-week siege, opening the St Lawrence for the attack on Quebec.
William Henry Harrison’s troops repulsed an attack by warriors of Tecumseh’s confederacy near Prophetstown in Indiana; ‘Tippecanoe and Tyler too’ later helped win him the presidency.

event: A Vodou ceremony launches the Haitian Revolution
note: Enslaved leaders met in a forest clearing near Cap-Français (Cap-Haïtien), traditionally at Bois Caïman, where Dutty Boukman called for the revolt that became the Haitian Revolution.

event: San Martín wins the Battle of Maipú
note: José de San Martín’s army defeated the royalists on the plain of Maipú, south-west of Santiago, securing Chile’s independence.

event: Chilean troops storm the Morro of Arica
note: In the War of the Pacific, Chilean infantry took the fortified headland above the port of Arica in under an hour; the city has been Chilean ever since.
King Oswiu of Northumbria chose Roman rather than Irish custom for dating Easter at a council in Abbess Hild’s monastery on the Yorkshire coast.

event: Pope Urban II calls for the First Crusade
note: At the end of a church council at Clermont in the Auvergne, Urban II preached to a crowd in a field outside the city, which answered ‘Deus vult!’ (God wills it).
Kitchener confronted Captain Marchand’s small French expedition at the ruined fort of Fashoda on the White Nile; France backed down, and Sudan stayed under British control.

event: Yuri Gagarin lands after the first human spaceflight
note: Gagarin ejected from Vostok 1 and parachuted into a field near Engels in the Saratov region; a farmer and her granddaughter were the first to greet him.

event: Burke and Wills reach the northern coast of Australia
note: Robert O’Hara Burke and William Wills reached the tidal mangroves near the Gulf of Carpentaria, completing the first south-to-north crossing of Australia; both died on the way back.

event: Çatalhöyük, one of the first towns, is founded
note: One of the world’s earliest towns grew on the Konya plain in central Anatolia; its people entered their mud-brick houses through the roof and buried their dead beneath the floors.

event: Australians hold the Kokoda Track at Isurava
note: Outnumbered Australian militia and AIF battalions fought a Japanese force in the Owen Stanley Range at Isurava, a key stand in the defence of Port Moresby.
The largest land battle before 1914 was fought outside Mukden (Shenyang) in Manchuria; Japan’s victory over Russia came at enormous cost to both sides.
Prussia’s victory near the Bohemian village of Sadová (Sadowa), north-west of Königgrätz (Hradec Králové), settled which power would unite Germany.
British and Indian forces besieged in the Manipur valley around Imphal held out until the Japanese offensive collapsed, in what was later voted Britain’s greatest battle.

event: Dmitry Donskoy defeats the Golden Horde
note: Grand Prince Dmitry of Moscow defeated the Tatar commander Mamai on the Kulikovo Field near the upper Don, south of Tula, a symbol of Russia’s rise against the Horde.
Alexander Nevsky’s Novgorodians defeated the Teutonic Knights on the frozen Lake Peipus, between modern Estonia and Russia; the exact spot on the lake is unknown.
A Polish–Lithuanian army under Władysław II Jagiełło crushed the Teutonic Knights between the villages of Grunwald and Stębark in Prussia, one of medieval Europe’s largest battles.
Quarrymen near Taung in South Africa found the skull of a young child that Raymond Dart named Australopithecus africanus, the first early human ancestor found in Africa.
Robert Baden-Powell’s garrison held the railway town of Mafeking for 217 days against the Boers; news of its relief set off wild celebrations in Britain.

event: Mexico cedes California to the United States
note: Mexico gave up about half its territory in a treaty signed at Guadalupe Hidalgo, beside the great shrine just north of Mexico City.

event: Ramesses II fights the Hittites at Kadesh
note: Probably the largest chariot battle ever fought, on the Orontes River in western Syria. Both sides claimed victory, and it led to one of the earliest surviving peace treaties; the city’s site is Tell Nebi Mend.
Alexander crossed the swollen Jhelum (Hydaspes) in a storm and defeated Porus and his war elephants in the Punjab; the crossing point, probably near Jalalpur, is disputed.

The Mauryan emperor’s conquest of Kalinga, on India’s east coast, was so bloody that he renounced war and turned to Buddhism; his edicts are carved on a rock at Dhauli, near the traditional battlefield.

event: Tipu Sultan dies defending his capital
note: British troops stormed Tipu Sultan’s island fortress of Seringapatam in the Kaveri river near Mysore; Tipu was killed fighting at the breach.

event: A typhoon wrecks Kublai Khan’s invasion fleet
note: The ‘kamikaze’, or divine wind, destroyed the Mongol fleet sheltering off Takashima island in Imari Bay, Kyushu, where archaeologists have since found its wrecks.

event: The Knights of St John withstand a great Ottoman siege
note: In the Great Siege of Malta, the Knights and the Maltese held Birgu and Fort St Angelo for four months against a huge Ottoman force; Valletta was built across the Grand Harbour afterwards.

event: Nelson destroys Napoleon’s fleet at anchor
